Let S be a compact Riemann surface of genus g greater than or equal to 1, 
and L a general element of the third Grassmannian for S. If T T' is a
non-singular pair of linear mappings from the sheaf of sections H^1(S, O) to
itself, then the image of the twisted attribute _twistedL(T') of the
bundle L when subjected to the attribute T is equal to L. Furthermore, 
for a general element T in the group PGL(3, Z[G_S]) where G_S is the
alternating group of degree 6, the twisted attribute _twistedL(T) for
L is not isomorphic to L. Moreover, an integral basis for H^1(S, O)(3) can
be found which remains invariant under the action of the group T, and this
result generalizes to a theorem for a specific geometric quadric by the
work of R. Laza and C. Paquette.

For the Q-function, which is closely tied to the error probability in communication systems, 
we establish its continuous derivative at each point, 
along with uniform convergence near infinity. Additionally, 
we derive its expansion into a power series along with a similar result for the modified Q-function.

This research explores the optical interaction between a dimer of dielectric nanoparticles near a graphene layer. By applying the multiple dipole approximation and incorporating the effects of graphene surface plasmons, we calculated the optical force acting on each nanoparticle. Our findings reveal that the oscillations of the graphene's surface plasmons can create an extremely strong attractive force between the nanoparticles, which could be many orders of magnitude greater than typical optical forces in other materials. We also demonstrated that the force's magnitude can be controlled by adjusting the graphene's dielectric properties via chemical doping or other methods. Additionally, we discovered that achieving this strong attraction likely requires nanoparticles with extremely small sizes, on the order of 10 nanometers, and operating frequencies very close to the resonant terahertz range.

The Emergency Department functions under severe time constraints, rendering the usual application of the average rate law ineffective. To rectify this issue, the theory of reaction rates is reexamined to account for the inherent time dependence inherent in emergencies. As a result, the concept of average reaction curves is developed to facilitate the calculation of treatment durations within this time frame. Specifically, the calculated data is based on the intersection points between the ET and AT curves, enabling the determination of upper and lower limits for treatment durations. To verify the efficacy of this new framework, the proposed method is tested using simulated data based on the rates of emergency occurrence and treatment duration. To address the non-uniform distribution of emergencies, the theoretical framework is further adapted to accommodate this non-uniformity, yielding an analytical solution for the overall treatment duration in this modified scenario.

This research focuses on the development of a communication protocol allowing a group of robots to simultaneously execute multiple tasks by synchronizing their actions in conjunction with an external leader. A collective task is defined as an objective that requires all robots to perform the same sequence of tasks in the same order. Exploiting the properties of regular networks and the robots' limited capabilities, we devise a distributed algorithm that enables a group of robots to execute collective tasks in a stable and efficient manner. Furthermore, we provide theoretical justification for the algorithm's efficacy and prove its convergence to the desired task implementation for networks lacking persistent active cycles and a corresponding graph representation known as the two-cycles graph. To tackle the general case involving any regular graph, we divide it into smaller components by partitioning the graph and design an algorithm that achieves task implementation within these partitioned components. Finally, we apply this approach to an extended model that incorporates time delays in communication processes.

Research has examined the event shape and azimuthal correlations in Pb-Pb collisions at 2.76 and 5.02 TeV to explore the chiral magnetic effect's (CME) impact on charged particles. The study utilized the ALICE detector and analyzed collisions with at least two charged particles, focusing on in-plane and out-of-plane events. The findings show that the CME's influence does not significantly contribute to the correlations studied. The measured effects were consistent with those seen in proton-proton collisions, with peripheral collisions exhibiting slightly higher correlations than central collisions, likely caused by statistical fluctuations. Furthermore, simulations by TYIGM and CHM v2 suggest that CME's impact is largely masked by background effects such as the scalar CME and correlations related to anisotropic flow.

For online fundraising to be successful, it's crucial to understand the real-time crowd reactions to ongoing campaigns, allowing for precise and timely adjustments to be made. Research into crowd reactions is further complicated by the influence of biases such as selection bias - where only certain data is presented, and presentation bias - the way in which data is displayed. This study focuses on crowdfunding and utilizes a novel, multi-platform analysis that incorporates various biases. The researchers found that real-time crowd reactions are highly predictive of whether a campaign will be successful. More specifically, the highest correlation with fundraising outcomes was found in the time period immediately following the initial video on crowdfunding platforms, suggesting that videos are a crucial factor in determining crowdfunding success. The researchers also discovered that the magnitude of crowd reactions can accurately estimate the likelihood of a campaign's success.

Machine learning (ML) based detection of network attacks has become more effective with the use of deep learning (DL) techniques. However, the effectiveness of ML and DL models in this context can be significantly enhanced through the exchange of data and knowledge among security experts. This exchange raises concerns regarding the security of the shared data due to the potential for inversion attacks. To address these concerns, this research proposes a novel federated learning framework that enables security organizations to collaborate on training without compromising their data. The proposed framework is complemented by an intrusion detection system (IDS) built with convolutional neural networks, which serves as a test model to demonstrate the efficacy of this collaboration. The results show that federated learning can yield an accuracy of 98% for detecting nine types of network attacks, outperforming the accuracy achieved through traditional means of data sharing and knowledge exchange.

The issue of task sequencing in robotic manufacturing encompasses both the assignment of tasks to robotic stations and the determination of a feasible and efficient sequence of tasks for each station. To tackle this challenge, a sequential approach is typically insufficient, necessitating a more comprehensive solution. We present a novel grouping-based algorithm that addresses task assignment and sequencing concurrently, aiming to minimize overall production time and maximize robotic utilization. The proposed method incorporates a greedy strategy for generating groups and calculating corresponding group execution times. Furthermore, the algorithm distributes tasks in a balanced manner across robotic stations to maximize efficiency and predictability in manufacturing operations. The proposed solution outperforms existing methods, as confirmed by simulation outcomes using real-world data from the YO1 enterprise.

The performance of the interface between semiconductors and barriers is a crucial factor in producing reliable, quantum-coherent electronic components. A key aspect is the type of semiconductor material used, particularly its dopant type, concentration, and depth below the barrier material. In this research, advanced SiMOSFETs were used, utilizing a full 300mm CMOS process with a molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) grown GaAs crystal and a controlled SiMOSFET channel. A significant increase in electron mobility was observed in the SiMOSFETs following an ultra-thin oxide gate treatment, demonstrating the potential for high performance in quantum devices when combining advanced SiMOSFETs with sophisticated epitaxial barriers.

Human communicators can efficiently exchange information across diverse platforms, unlike machines, which struggle to compensate for discrepancies in input and output systems. Inspired by social networks, researchers have developed a new approach to address this challenge by leveraging a theory called group harmony in social networks. Through computational simulations, this method has shown potential in achieving stable equilibrium states that enable secure and efficient data exchange. Additionally, the experiment revealed that the underlying graph structure in these networks plays a crucial role in achieving harmony, and these findings have been substantiated by theoretical proofs. Consequently, the outcomes of this study offer significant insights for designing machine group communications that can effectively handle parameter discrepancies.

Our study examines the existence of source bias in video search outcomes by investigating how the source can influence the likelihood of a video being recommended. We found that video upload motivations such as monetization and peer influence can lead to differences in source bias. To tackle this issue, we propose a new approach that uses the concept of normality to quantify the degree of source bias. This method relies on the creation of a normalisation model that uses source information to determine whether a video's engagement comes from its source-related attributes or the content itself. However, our results reveal that current normalisation models are unable to fully eliminate source bias, suggesting the need for further research in this area.

A new method has been developed to create monodromy defects in 2+1D topological orders using Wilson lines, which can be applied to both the Wess-Zumino model and other types of topological orders. This technique combines the advantages of the level/k modular fusion framework and the quantum information concept of entanglement bootstrap. The monodromy defects created through this method can be used to construct topological orders with multiple distinct factors, such as $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$ and U(1). The technique also allows for the precise calculation of fusion spaces and branching rules. Furthermore, the closure conditions for the monodromy defects can be used to construct defects in the original Wess-Zumino model, which can be related to the bosonic part of the holographic duals of the free theories.

We have found 10 elliptic curves defined over cyclic cubic fields with a point of rank 13, and as these ranks are influenced by the 3-Selmer rank for isogeny $\eta_3 = [3, 3]$ and due to the non-existence of 3-torsion points on these curves, this provides further confirmation for the theory proposed by Fukuda and pre-existing results from Katsuragi, which stated that the rank of an elliptic curve with a 3-torsion point is maximized at 12.

The interference pattern is a key factor in the analysis and optimization of wireless networks. However, the standard methods for describing interference, such as using distances or signal-to-interference ratios, are insufficient for solving certain optimization problems. To address this issue, a novel approach is presented that models interference as a result of random medium access scheduling. This framework offers a more detailed and precise representation of interference, enabling the solution of previously intractable optimization problems related to wireless network resource allocation. The proposed method is versatile and can be applied to various interference patterns and resource allocation challenges, with a specific example given in the paper.

Current Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) rely on node labels during training, which involves propagating label information through edges. However, acquiring and utilizing node labels in many real-world scenarios is impractical due to the effort and cost involved. To address this challenge, we present a novel approach that leverages a degree-based pseudo-tagging method to train GNNs effectively with only a few labels. Our approach employs a simple, efficient strategy to assign multiple pseudo-nodes to unlabelled nodes based on their edge connections, which helps to expand labelled areas and effectively segment graphs. Notably, our method outperforms existing approaches in multiple benchmark datasets, as well as a recently proposed method that also relies on pseudo-nodes.

In video processing tasks, adjacent frames often contain redundant information that can be leveraged to enhance performance, but current models typically discard this spatial context in favor of focusing solely on temporal relationships. To capitalize on both spatial and temporal connections within video sequences, we introduce the PatchNet structure, allowing it to retain and synthesize frame features through the utilization of sliding patch matching and aggregation techniques. By incorporating key technological advancements, such as multi-level patch refinement and high-resolution feature handling, the PatchNet architecture enables the efficient handling of large-scale video datasets. As a result, it outperforms state-of-the-art models in various video-based applications like semantic segmentation, object detection, and video semantic segmentation, with notable improvements in runtime efficiency as well. The source code of the PatchNet framework is available at https://github.com/chenyilong/patchnet.

We examine the one-dimensional asymmetric exclusion process with transition rates based on a real number $q$ and examine the $n$-point function for a specific situation where the process has reached a stationary state with $q$ as its primary parameter. For the case when $q$ is not located on the real axis, or if it is located but does not equal -1/4, we derive mathematically exact formulas describing how probabilities of certain arrangements of particles at different points in the system vary with the length of the system. These arrangements correspond to a specific state, denoted as $\tau_n$, which has particles moving in the opposite direction. Our paper builds upon a formula for the two-point function, previously established by Bouchitté et al., by first proving a formula for the difference between the logarithm of a specific probability and the logarithm of a related probability, both occurring within the system: this specific probability is calculated as the product of transition probabilities, while the related probability is calculated as the product of similar probabilities, but with some of the particles' states changed. This formula involves the inverse of a specific matrix. Our paper then partitions the one-point function into two components, by first expressing it as the sum of a series, which converges to a specific probability, which we have previously determined to be related to a specific state, and then showing that the difference between this one-point function and the previously established formula is proportional to the logarithm of the system's

A new method of addressing the significant power consumption issue in future wireless networks is through the use of energy-harvesting technology, specifically in a system where data is transmitted via wireless signals, known as the power transfer over communication tradeoff. This concept is realized through a power transfer model that depends on the same frequencies as the communication system, enabling devices to harness energy from the received signals while still maintaining data transmission. In order to optimize this energy-harvesting process, a novel access technique is developed, allowing multiple users to simultaneously receive both power and data from a single set of access points while minimizing interference. As a result, a multi-variable optimization problem is formulated to maximize the overall data rate in the system. Since the problem is shown to be non-convex in certain situations, a suitable reformulation is presented to make it convex, followed by the derivation of an iterative algorithm designed to resolve this optimization problem. The algorithm is proven to converge to an optimal solution, providing a viable strategy for realizing the SWIPT concept. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through numerical simulations that highlight its practical applicability and the substantial data rate improvements it can achieve under various system configurations.

In Fermi gases with low concentrations of magnetic properties, a particular model, called the SU(N) Pauli model, is frequently utilized for the theoretical analysis of magnetic properties. This paper addresses the question of whether a more comprehensive theoretical model, which incorporates both magnetic properties and the tendency of particles to avoid each other, can provide similar predictions for magnetic properties. To answer this question, we first modify the more comprehensive theoretical model to duplicate the assumptions of the SU(N) Pauli model and demonstrate that, at extremely low concentrations of magnetic properties, the two models yield identical results for certain characteristics. Additionally, we expand the more comprehensive theoretical model to incorporate more detailed effects of particle interactions and utilize numerical methods to investigate the characteristics of this expanded model. To confirm the characteristics of the expanded model, we compare its predictions with experimental data and find a satisfactory agreement.

We develop a classical electrical circuit model for certain types of electromagnetic interactions within microwave optomechanics. Specifically, we're looking at a specific setup that includes a mechanical resonance and two coupled optical resonators. Our electrical circuit equivalent uses a mixture of linear capacitive and resistive damping to model the mechanical resonance and predictive protocols are developed to analyze electrical circuit behavior for detecting mechanical phenomena. The individual optical resonators are represented as parallel RLC circuits, highlighting the distinct effects of coupling on back-action and heating. The developed model aids in understanding the general optomechanical interaction and also presents a new method for analysis and optimization.

Properties of semi-infinite rationally charged rectangular targets are examined 
using the generalized Airy polynomial framework, which incorporates supplementary 
parameters to the traditional Airy polynomial, enabling a comprehensive study 
through symbolic computations with the Casimir operator. This analysis reveals 
detailed information about energy levels, associated states and spatial distribution 
of the charge. The study also explores connections with other, specific models, 
including the infinite q-deformed harmonic oscillator, the generalized deformed 
Hahn polynomials, the generalized deformed Hulthén potential, the generalized 
deformed Poschl-Teller potential, the generalized deformed Morse potential, the 
asymmetric Coulomb potential, the effective potential of the two-dimensional 
ideal Bose gas, the effective potential of the two-dimensional ideal fermi gas, 
notably that the generalized Airy polynomials produce real or imaginary values for 
the energy quantums, depending on the sign of specific parameters. 
Additionally, the study examines the physical implications of zero-charge energy 
quantums in the context of the Coulomb system.

Our research focuses on an obstacle following robot's navigation using only a map, which we refer to as the RFM. The obstacle following approach simplifies the navigation challenge for the robot, allowing it to move efficiently along the wall in a crowded environment. Similar to other swarm behaviors, the situation becomes complex if the robot and other obstacles move randomly. This chaotic movement leads to an exploration of the parameter space for the number of robots and their movement patterns. Through this investigation, we observe that the system undergoes an unexpected shift from collaborative to competitive behavior, characterized by a gap in the response times for various numbers of robots. To understand this phenomenon, we analyzed the system's dynamics mathematically and confirmed our findings through extensive computer simulations. Interestingly, the transition occurs at a number of robots that is a multiple of the number of degrees of freedom in the system's state space.

This article further develops and refines the concept of chiral aspects in 2dcft within the pAQFT framework, expanding upon a concept initially explored in arXiv:2103.01367. The chiral aspects are represented by a collection of represntations, known as the chiral algebra $\mathcal{A}$, in a suitable gauge, which enables the analysis of the massless sector through the study of the exchange algebras and their applications. The findings include the identification of the radiative degree of freedom and the exploration of the properties of the exchange algebras. The results show that the structure of the exchange algebras is completely determined by the properties of the chiral algebra's subalgebras, allowing for a new perspective on the concept of "observed" degree of freedom in the context of 2dcft.

Improving surgical outcomes with high-quality video is reliant on effective smoke removal methods to prevent the hazardous effects of surgical smoke on health. Current smoke detection techniques are limited by their susceptibility to optical interferences resulting from the smoky environment. To address this challenge, a novel smoke classification framework is introduced, utilizing a dual approach that combines smoke characteristics derived from image processing with smoke features extracted from RGB data through a CNN. Notably, the framework's first component is unaffected by the interferences that plague traditional RGB-based methods. Extensive testing on a substantial dataset of real-world smoke images demonstrates the framework's superior smoke detection capabilities.

Our research presents a strategy for creating stable, single-qubit gates using the M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gate operation, utilizing multiple vibrational modes in an trap. This approach distributes the modulation of the gate across several phonons to counteract the influence of drive frequency deviations. A demonstration of this concept is carried out using a range of experiments involving up to five distinct vibrational modes in a range of 1 to 20 MHz, set up in an ion trap system. The implementation of this idea significantly reduces the magnitude of effects which limit the quantum gate's duration, thus making it suitable for applications involving large numbers of qubits and numerous vibrational modes.

To address the scarcity of accurate computer models for paraelectric materials like BaTiO$3$, we've developed a novel approach. We utilized a template-based method to create a large number of microscopically detailed crystal structures, which were subsequently refined using neural networks. This unprecedented collection of paraelectric structures serves as a foundation for addressing long-standing problems in materials science, including the lack of reliable experimental and theoretical data and the challenges of modeling phase transitions and polarization properties.

Multivariate data that change over space or time can often be analyzed with a statistical model known as multivariate Gaussian processes (GP). Researchers recently developed the concept of functional Gaussian process (FGP) to analyze such data by first breaking it down into smaller sections or'segments', and then modeling the relationships between these segments using a statistical model called the functional Gaussian graphical model (FGGM). This new approach allows researchers to identify the connections and groups within the data more clearly. A similar idea was introduced as the graphical Gaussian process (GGP) which uses a statistical model to analyze relationships between various'segments' of GP parameters. This paper explores the theoretical connections between FGGP and GGP, and reveals that they express essentially the same idea when using a specific representation of functional data known as the state-space representation. Additionally, our study extends this idea to estimate the structure of GP covariances using functional principal component analysis and reveals that both approaches reveal similar results when applied to the same data.

This paper examines the challenges of mapping quantum circuits to the hardware architecture, specifically the tile structure, and introduces two novel, deterministic methods for circuit compilation based on pattern matching and the application of group invariants. These methods guarantee the generation of valid tiles in all cases, unlike probabilistic approaches that rely on the circuit's recurrence pattern and the number of distinct gates in the circuit's source. Our experiments involve simulating the behavior of circuits with varying levels of recurrence and an increasing number of distinct gates, comparing the computational complexity of the two deterministic methods and the probabilistic approach. Furthermore, we conduct a practical evaluation of the two deterministic methods against the established probabilistic method, using a diverse set of quantum circuits to determine their accuracy and efficiency. Our findings suggest that the probabilistic method outperforms the deterministic methods, but the difference in FLOPs is relatively small and the deterministic methods have the advantage of guaranteed success. Our study also provides insights for the development of more efficient deterministic methods, specifically the need to further optimize the pattern matching process or by leveraging symmetry in the circuit compilation process.

A recent approach to optimizing techniques employs average-case (a.k.a. Bayesian) modeling, using explicit probability distributions over potential input data. This paper's key findings are two-fold. First, we establish that the convex optimization technique, utilizing a drillable objective function and an elastic net regularization component, exhibits average-case universality across a broad family of probability distributions. Secondly, at nearly optimal regularization parameters, the same technique exhibits average-case robustness to perturbations within a related family of Epsilon-spheres, specifically in scenarios utilizing Gaussian noise models. This research significantly expands upon the current knowledge in this domain, offering the first instance of a single optimization technique to display both average-case universality and robustness across various noise models. Additionally, our study provides the first robustness guarantee to be related to the statistical variance of the underlying distribution it seeks to optimize.

Recent breakthroughs in producing artificial two-dimensional materials with specifically designed atomic structures have brought us closer to achieving a solid state equivalent of the double layer excitonic insulator, a concept that has been consistently observed in one-dimensional systems but not in two-dimensional ones. Despite the advancements, the challenge of controlling the environment to ensure a stable insulating state remains unresolved. In this study, we simulate the optical properties of a double layer excitonic insulator comprised of alternating barium and titanium dioxides, and our results show that the excitonic features observed in the photoemission spectra and optical conductivity strongly rely on the placement of a superfluid cuprate layer between the barium and titanium dioxides. Additionally, we find that the excitonic weights of the emitted light have a tendency to increase when the layers are positioned further apart, reminiscent of the behavior observed in one-dimensional systems. These findings support the idea that a double layer excitonic insulator can be achieved through the creation of complex two-dimensional structures with controlled interfaces.

We have developed an adaptive algorithm for estimating the position and movement of targets in areas with multiple mobile propagation paths and diverse channel conditions. This non-linear prediction and tracking method employs radio waves to determine the location of targets, similar to the well-known Kalman filter but with a unique advantage in the context of channelized radio communication. To leverage the strengths of radio waves in channelized environments, the algorithm incorporates the characteristics of wave propagation and the dynamics of target movement. This results in higher accuracy of position estimates compared to a conventional Kalman filter, with the added benefit of robust performance across various channel conditions.

The joint polarization of $W$ and $Z$ bosons is studied in $pp$ collisions at a 13 TeV energy threshold using the LHCb detector as a polarimeter. This is achieved by analyzing the angular correlations between $W$ and $Z$ bosons produced via the $pp \rightarrow WZ$ reaction and created in events with three charged leptons and missing energy. A total of 1.8 femtobarns of integrated luminosity from 2015 to 2018 is used in the study. A theoretical model based on the standard model is used to determine the joint polarization states of $W$ and $Z$ bosons, taking into account previous studies on gauge boson polarization states. The joint polarization states of $W$ and $Z$ bosons are found to be in agreement with the standard model predictions.

The fabric tensor is an novel frame-determining approach that describes a complex phenomenon like viscosity by relating it to the directional interactions within a given frame. This methodology can be applied to a complex phenomenon like gravity and its influence on space-time for identifying a suitable directional approach. The fabric tensor for gravity is heavily dependent on how its components are defined in relation to the gravitational field's directional aspects. A preliminary mathematical framework for the fabric tensor of gravity has been developed using the concept of auto-regressive moving-average processes in relation to the gravitational potential's time series. The gravity tensor's fabric can be represented by a matrix calculus-based statistical method called cross spectral density, which analyzes the directional interactions between different frequency components of the gravitational potential. A hypothetical scenario of gravity-drenched solution with directional gravitational properties is used for illustrating the methodology of determining the fabric tensor of gravity.

We introduce a subcategory of Orlo consisting of full lattices, where the morphisms are preserved in both directions, and demonstrate that every orthomodular lattice has an associated topological system that is both simple and meet-complete. In this context, we define the category Orlo_top and show that it has a dual for every orthomodolar lattice within it. Additionally, for certain extended forms of orthomodular lattices, we establish the topological system's uniqueness.

We introduce a visual representation system that translates Coq proof scripts into tabular forms, which can be exported as $\LaTeX$ or PDF files. Our tool aims to facilitate learning and proof review by providing an interactive visual representation of each step in a proof. Consequently, this system enables educators and reviewers to utilize the proofs without relying on the Coq program, thereby making it easier to understand the proofs using only a web browser. Additionally, this system can be accessed through a web interface at https://coq-psv.github.io/coq-psv/.

We demonstrate that the fourth moment of holomorphic Hecke cusp forms, as defined by Iwaniec and Szeidl, undergoes a sharp transformation at the critical strip's edge, $s=1$. This involves proving they have a limit of $\pi^{2p}\cdot(2p-1)!\cdot \Gamma(2p)$ as $s$, or the associated real part, tends towards one from the negative side. This confirms conjectures made by Christoffel, Runge, and Vinogradov, as well as settling the question posed by Li in 2018 for this specific type of cusp forms, also resolving the issue raised by Christianson in 2019, by providing an alternative solution to his question. In this paper, we present a novel strategy to conclude the inner iterations in Interior Point Methods by contrasting the residual norms of consecutive iterations. Specifically, we leverage the Ritz vector properties to connect the primal and dual residuals, enabling us to terminate inner iterations by checking if the primal residual has diminished sufficiently. This approach is initially outlined for Quantum Mechanical problems and then expanded to general Interior Point Methods, encompassing a wide range of applications, including to SVMs, matching problems, and others. We demonstrate that this method is effective in reducing the total iteration count while maintaining comparable computational efficiency for IPMs.

We have derived the $A_{gq}^{(8)}$ function to the third order in $\alpha_s$ with its polarized part, allowing the creation of a novel function, $A_{gq}(N)$, through the FF scheme, enabling the transition from $A_{gq}^{\rm (T)}$ to $A_{gq}(N)$. This gives us the ability to analyze contributions from single-anomalous-parton-number corrections and $N$-dependent scale choices, facilitating the understanding of scale-dependent effects in different parton-model quantities. Additionally, the new $A_{gq}(N)$ function empowers the implementation of the Variable Flavor Number Scheme (VFNS) at $O(\alpha_s^3)$, aiding in the accurate matching of different scale choices in different quark-flavor regions, as required in modern PDF fits with $\alpha_s(m_Z^2) \simeq 0.1187$ and inclusion of $A_{gq}(N)$ terms in these analyses.

Established industries such as aviation and healthcare have learned from compiling databases of incidents to avoid replicating errors, thereby reducing future incidents. Conversely, the field of AI is lacking in systematic knowledge management to prevent and mitigate failures. A rich ecosystem of AI technologies exists, encompassing various applications and knowledge domains, yet there is no centralized resource to document critical incidents related to AI system operation. To address this knowledge management gap in AI, we have created the AI Incident Database (AIDb), a knowledge base of reported AI failures and near-misses, along with accompanying articles and research papers. The AIDb aims to prevent and mitigate future AI failures by enabling lessons from past incidents to be applied to the development and operation of AI systems.

The principle behind the renormalization group can be satisfied with an exact change of variables that masks the physical details of a system, unlike approximate methods such as perturbation theory where the renormalization group is often applied. A new algorithm has been created to carry out this transformation exactly using a formulation similar to gradient descent, allowing the emergence of a phase transition or critical point when the flow reaches a point where the system's self-similarity is preserved. This exact renormalization group technique is capable of handling complex systems, such as the Kondo problem, where a perturbation theory approach fails to accurately describe the system's behavior below a certain temperature threshold without resorting to approximate methods like perturbation theory or the multi-scale renormalization group technique.

Current business process monitoring methods mainly concentrate on one process model. However, in some scenarios, it is necessary to analyze multiple process descriptions together, such as tracing execution gaps between them or identifying clashes between them. This requires not only individual model monitoring but also the detection of conflicts between these models. This research proposes a new method that uses a monitoring approach based on automata to tackle the problem of aligning multiple process definitions and detecting their clashes. The method is also adaptable to handle discrepancies in performance and coverage when comparing models. The feasibility of this method is demonstrated through the analysis of the complexity involved. This research was initially presented at the BPM 2020 PhD Symposium as a short paper and is now expanded into a full paper, addressing additional comments and insights from the panel.

Quipper, a domain-specific language, is designed to efficiently create and operate on quantum circuits. Its compiler translates the code into executable quantum programs runnable on existing quantum devices. The language's static type system and abstract machine in Quipper ensure program correctness by verifying that the program's behavior matches its specifications, which is later confirmed when compiling the program to quantum code that can be executed on real or simulated quantum devices. The advancement of quantum technology makes it crucial to develop more sophisticated tools for programming quantum devices accurately. Building upon the established foundation of Quipper, a more advanced version of the language is developed to provide more sophisticated programming features. This enhanced version incorporates higher-order functions, recursion, and a more robust type system with the ability to include arbitrary functions in types. The corresponding abstract machine for this upgraded language is also introduced, which is based on a higher-order abstract machine design. The paper describes the improved language and its associated machine with the help of a detailed formal interpretation that relates the language's syntax to its semantics. Additionally, the paper establishes a proof of correctness for the compilation process from the upgraded Quipper code to quantum programs runnable on real or simulated quantum devices. The improved version of Quipper expands the possibilities for expressing quantum algorithms and provides a higher level of abstraction than the original Quipber, while the corresponding abstract machine indicates that the programs are executed on a virtual abstract processor.

In the realm of random matrix theory, researchers have demonstrated that the extreme statistics of GOE and GUE matrices exhibit similar behavior outside of their respective critical points. This finding suggests that there are two distinct regimes: one where the statistics are linearly related and another where they follow a power law distribution. Despite the differing natures of these regimes, researchers have successfully mapped the local properties of these statistics to those of the 3D Ising model near its critical point. This mapping allows researchers to leverage the sophisticated understanding of the 3D Ising model to gain insights into the statistical distribution of the matrix's extremes. This level of understanding has been elusive in the study of matrix extremes thus far. Researchers have derived a universal distribution that describes the distribution of the matrix's extremes across various ensembles, including GOE, GUE, and GSE. This work represents a significant advancement in the field, bridging the gap between theoretical and numerical approaches to study matrix extremes.

To enhance the precision of optical measurements, we explore a novel approach that utilizes ensembles of $^{148}\textrm{Nd}^+$ ions, leveraging their exceptionally long-lived dipole moments coupled to an on-resonance cavity. A plan to utilize bosonic pairs and squeezing concepts is outlined to attain highly correlated states, thereby amplifying the cavity's quantum field and thereby optimizing the optical magnetometer sensitivity. We outline the necessary cooling and manipulation protocols using both laser-based and cavity-driven Raman transitions to achieve the desired pair generation and squeezing goals. We also address the essential need for quantum control at the ensemble level to overcome single-particle interfering effects, thereby enabling the optimization of pair generation and squeezing parameters within the acceptable ion loss timeframe.

Assembling a complete genome from short, overlapping DNA sequences is a critical yet computationally complex task within the genomics pipeline. Due to the rapidly expanding genomic dataset, high-performance and scalable approaches are essential for managing the increased computational demands. A novel, parallel algorithm is proposed, using a graph representation and sparse matrices to create continuous, overlapping DNA sequences within a chromosomal region. By dividing the genome into fixed-size segments and assigning them to processors, the algorithm efficiently creates contigs through sparse matrix computations. Through performance evaluations on various genomes and architectures, the proposed method demonstrates significant speedups, achieving up to 82x improvement on 80 cores for the human genome, outperforming a current solution that only reaches 5.8x speedup on 80 cores. Additionally, the new approach significantly reduces memory usage, lowering global memory access for graph node insertion and abating the slowdown due to increasing genome sizes.

A logarithmic delay logistic equation, relevant to cell biology, is analyzed to study its nonlinear dynamics. The equation's right side involves a logarithmic function of the population size with a delay. The global behavior of this delay-based logistic equation is equivalent to that of the standard logistic equation but with a discontinuity at zero population size. The global stability of its equilibrium points is examined by solving the equation for certain boundary values of the delay parameter and its positive solutions. The study reveals that the equation's solutions exhibit rapid and oscillatory behavior with increasing population size for small delay periods and certain conditions, including a condition for the standard logistic equation to apply. The implications of the delay term on the equation's dynamics are also discussed.

We introduce a novel framework to measure the depth of an arbitrary point process, enabling the identification of the deepest process. This approach leverages a distribution's layout in a specific basis, allowing us to extend the Isometric Log-Ratio transformation from multinomial distributions to an arbitrary point process. By applying the ILR transformation to a temporal Poisson process, we establish a depth-based ranking that coincides with the process's regularity in the time domain. Additionally, our method enables the determination of the deepest process in the context of time-series data, demonstrating its efficacy through the analysis of synthetic data that showcases its ability to differentiate between various Gaussian time-series models.

Achieving significant practical benefits from superconducting technologies often relies on creating efficient converters of electrical to mechanical and thermal energy. For this purpose, we combine superconducting materials, demonstrating an ideal integration of quantum limits on heat and mechanical energy consumption. The resulting system consists of an optomechanical device, in which an optical cavity and a granular superconducting bulk form a hybrid entity. The optical cavity acts as an electrical signal input, while the superconducting bulk acts as a mechanical sensor that converts residual heat into a measurable property. The research shows that even in the presence of minor imperfections and electrical resistance, our hybrid device can successfully perform an electrical-to-mechanical energy conversion, paving the way for the practical utilization of superconducting materials in such implementations.

The AdaMIC gamma-ray detector was used to study the gamma-ray activity following the $^{42}\mathrm{Ge}(d,^{3}\mathrm{He}$) $^{40}\mathrm{Ge}$ fusion reaction at energy levels near the $N$ = 40 closure, which was investigated at a 15 UD cyclotron using 20-25 MeV dedicated beams. The newly discovered 1113 keV gamma ray was identified at 45.9% branching ratio, with the newly established 1113 keV gamma ray's placement detailed along with the previously identified 655 keV gamma ray's placement. The newly established 1113 keV gamma ray's placement detailed along with the previously identified 655 keV gamma ray's placement. A novel technique for accurately measuring the masses of extremely short-lived, unusual atomic isotopes over extended periods has been developed at the Lanzhou CSRC's Isotope Mass Spectrometry facility. This innovative method leverages the capabilities of a specific type of atomic beam separator, operating in an isochronous mode, to pinpoint masses with extraordinary precision. With the ability to process large quantities of ions at once and an automated system for handling samples, this technique enables the mass measurement of a wide range of isotopes, from well-known variants to those that have never before been studied. As part as a international collaboration, this technique was utilized to measure the mass of two extremely short-lived isotopes: $^{56}$Ca and $^{58}$Fe. The resulting data show a significant reduction in the current most commonly accepted mass values for these isotopes, further highlighting their unusual mass patterns.

Common computational methods in lattice field theories, such as Monte Carlo sampling, face challenges due to the significant computational time required, leading to the costly statistical error associated with these methods. In recent years, the development of graph neural networks has made it possible to utilize them as standardizers to eliminate this error, effectively exploiting the vast amount of computational resources available. However, utilizing these neural standardizers in practical lattice field theory simulations proves to be a complex task, largely due to the intricate nature of the simulations involved. In an effort to address this challenge, the Neural Standardizers for Lattice Field Theory (NSLFT) project has been established, aiming to provide standardized simulations for lattice field theory in an easily accessible manner. In line with this goal, the project includes a comprehensive suite of standardized simulations for a variety of lattice models, such as the U(1), Z(2), SU(N) group theories, as well as the Higgs and QCD models, with the associated documentation and software packages freely available for public use. In this study, we outline the conceptual framework of the NSLFT project, before systematically demonstrating the implementation of the graph neural network standardizer on the SU(N) lattice gauge theory model, specifically the SU(2) gauge theory model with pure and dynamical fermions. In line with the NSLFT's policy of transparency, the associated documentation and software packages, such as the standardized simulations, the graph neural network training, the data preprocessing and the visualization tools

This paper explores a novel approach to text recognition that utilizes pre-defined patterns to facilitate the extraction of structured information from unordered chips. The proposed method involves developing a biasing model that consists of a regular expression-based loss function and a novel extraction metric, both of which can be incorporated into the standard text recognition training process. The biasing model is initially applied to a small, annotated dataset and yields a set of pre-trained models, which can then be employed to identify suitable targets for the subsequent fine-tuning process. The research encompasses an extensive range of experiments on various datasets, as well as an in-depth analysis of the effectiveness of the biased target selection strategy. The findings reveal that the proposed method significantly enhances the accuracy of structured text extraction and provides more efficient target selection, thus accelerating the training process.

This study focuses on key entity recognition and relation detection, addressing the schema linking aspect of semantic interpretation, albeit from a unique perspective: utilizing a large collection of existing knowledge bases to define relationships rather than relying on dataset-specific annotations. To achieve this, our model incorporates three key components:

1.  **Relationship Inventory:** This step involves identifying relevant knowledge base relations applicable to a given text and filtering out irrelevant ones based on content.
2.  **Grid Attention:** This module arranges recognized entities and relationships in a grid structure, facilitating the analysis of their interactions and relative positions.
3.  **Auxiliary Visual Grounding:** This step integrates visual elements by incorporating an additional layer that incorporates image features, enhancing the model's ability to distinguish between relevant and irrelevant relationships.

Our novel approach's effectiveness is demonstrated through superior performance on datasets like SQA and TASS, showcasing significant improvements over state-of-the-art models. Additionally, our analytical comparisons highlight the model's ability to produce more accurate entity rankings and relation maps, cementing its position as a pioneering model in this domain.

The ongoing LoTSS survey is conducting a thorough observation of the Northern sky at 147 MHz to gather insights into the dynamic processes governing large-scale galaxy distributions. Through initial data analysis, researchers obtained 42,142 individual galaxy detections within a 222-square-degree area, each accompanied by accurate flux measurements and positional accuracy. To understand the relationship between galaxies and the mass distribution of the universe, scientists employed multi-dimensional fitting to determine redshifts for 19,071 galaxies from the LoTSS dataset. To verify their findings, the team completed cross-checks using multiple external data sources, including the SDSS DR12, UDS, and COSMOS surveys. Subsequent analysis led to the determination of linear biasing parameters for 13 galaxy samples, all of which exhibit consistent evolution. Furthermore, researchers discovered that these galaxies exhibit a typical linear bias of $3.3$ and that the bias increases with increasing stellar mass. Additionally, the team calculated the linear bias of LoTSS galaxies observed within specific redshift ranges, yielding an average linear bias of 3.3, 3.8, and 4.2 at redshifts 0.04, 0.2, and 0.3 respectively. Researchers used theoretical models to explain their findings, identifying mass-dependent bias as the primary factor driving their observations. Future data releases from LoTSS will encompass the entire Northern sky and incorporate 20% more galaxies, leading to enhanced insights and a significantly expanded understanding

Rank-structured and lasso-regulated models, such as the rank-lasso, are relatively unexplored, yet have tremendous potential in analyzing complex real-world data. The hybrid model, introduced recently, combines rank-lasso and lasso into a single framework, making it highly versatile and useful for a wide range of applications, taking linear regression as an example. The hybrid model offers significant benefits over other algorithms currently available in the field. To solve the hybrid model, a new adaptive-sieving-based algorithm, HyLasso+, has been developed, that is highly effective and takes into account the unique characteristics of the hybrid model. The HyLasso+ algorithm employs a two-stage adaptive-sieving approach to eliminate non-significant parameters, using a hybrid form of the lasso and rank-lasso objectives and an efficient adaptive procedure for parameter estimation. The HyLasso+ algorithm is capable of handling high-dimensional data and large datasets (millions of samples and features), as demonstrated by extensive simulation studies and real-world applications, including analysis of a complex disease and the prediction of continuous outcomes in a specific medical condition.

We examine a thermodynamic system that can be represented by a harmonic potential and its interaction with an oscillator bath for both weak and strong driving forces. We analyze the system's behavior during a Quench, a rapid change in the driving force, and find that the system always experiences an increase in entropy unless it reaches a equilibrium state. This irreversible process generates entropy, and we apply a convolution entropy approach to study the system's entropy creation during the Quench and a subsequent relaxation process. This technique allows us to investigate the influence of the driving force's amplitude and frequency on the system's entropy creation, and to compare it with the system's average thermal behavior for both weak and strong driving forces.

The beneficial influence of AI, notable in solving environmental issues, is increasingly being acknowledged. Nevertheless, a thorough examination of its overall effect on the environment has not been conducted so far. We aim to explore the hidden ecological consequences of AI-driven solutions designed to tackle environmental problems. To achieve this, we will analyze a comprehensive, dynamically evolving knowledge graph comprising 221 nodes and 943 edges, which encompasses key environmental factors and AI-driven solution attributes. To model and measure the ecological impacts of these solutions, we employ graph-based metrics, specifically the centrality measures. Our analysis, utilizing a complex network approach, enables us to uncover the previously unexamined environmental impacts of these solutions, which we anticipate will be highly valuable for both researchers and practitioners in the AI field.

This paper explores the emerging field of prescriptive process monitoring, which goes beyond descriptive and predictive processes. Prescriptive process monitoring not only forecasts issues but also offers pre-approved process modification suggestions to prevent forecasted problems. To illustrate the possibilities of prescriptive process monitoring, we developed a prototype system, known as the Prescriptive Process Monitor (PPM), which incorporates a predictive process model and a constraint-aware optimization engine. To showcase the effectiveness of PPM, we conducted a real-world experiment at an IT service company, allowing it to provide actionable process modification suggestions that increased process lead times and improved productivity while adhering to strict constraints.

This research introduces an innovative multigoal-oriented error control strategy tailored for solving Boussinesq problems with multiple goal functions. The goal functions we're focusing on are relative errors related to temperature distribution and flow velocity, which are significant in the context of the Boussinesq model. The technique utilizes a posteriori estimates that rely on the weak duality principle, with the goal of providing a lower bound for the relative error. The approach is to first divide the computational domain into smaller regions, then compute upper and lower bounds for the goal functions within those areas using finite element methods. The upper and lower bounds for the goal functions are then used to obtain a localized a posteriori error estimate. To validate our method, we tested it using the 2D Boussinesq equations with a heated cylinder problem and demonstrated its effectiveness in predicting the localized error. The study used adaptive mesh refinement to verify the accuracy of the error estimates and found that the method to be reliable.

Problems like Combined Bandwidth Packing, Combined Graph Orientation, Combined Traveling Salesman and Steiner Tree, and Combined Feedback Vertex Set, which involve selecting subsets in graphs for specific applications, exhibit similar properties and can be solved efficiently with specific polynomial-time algorithms when parameters are restricted to limited sizes. To compare their solutions with the basic versions of these problems, which have no obvious size limitations, we developed polynomial-time algorithms reducing the size of problem instances significantly by eliminating unnecessary elements. To validate the effectiveness of these reductions, we proved they do not affect the optimal solutions of the reduced and original problem instances.

We've explored a model where social network connections and personal opinions evolve in tandem. Our approach combines two established theories: the balance theory, which postulates that individuals with similar opinions tend to connect, and the limited confidence model, which simulates how people adjust their beliefs based on relationships. To understand how opinions and relationships interact, we developed a coupled system of which a particular version, the Jantbi model, is an extension. Through both the analysis of a homogeneous system and the examination of a heterogeneous version with two distinct groups, we observed that opinions converge to a stable state within a specific, balanced network configuration. Crucially, this equilibrium's relation to the initial states of both the network and the individuals' beliefs is defined by certain criteria, which also dictate the persistence of oscillating patterns when initially satisfied. Our findings also reveal that, in a system with two distinct groups, opinions in the smaller group are more susceptible to being swayed by the opposing group's opinions.

We've discovered asymptotically flat solutions for non-trivial, self-gravitating scalar fields in 4-dimensional space-time, resulting in stable configurations of scalar stars at their steady-state conditions. The system is governed by a complex set of nonlinear equations. However, due to the simplicity of the problem, it can be reduced to an ordinary differential equation for the scalar field, and an existing set of conditions previously outlined for the boundary conditions of hairy black holes can be applied, enabling the study of these scalar stars through analytical and numerical approaches.

Different genes exhibiting similar activation patterns may show distinct mRNA expression levels at different time points due to variations in RNA production and degradation rates. The influence of RNA splicing on transcription length cannot be ignored. Investigating the dynamics of RNA synthesis alone is essential to understand how cells regulate gene expression. We developed a new algorithm to analyze genomic data, accounting for characteristics of sampled time points, to determine the duration of RNA Complementary DNA (cDNA) production. Our model uses a piecewise-linear function to describe RNA-cDNA length relationships, allowing for the detection of production delays. Notably, applying this model to single-cell RNA-sequencing data from B cells and macrophages revealed considerable RNA production delays, predominantly in gene-rich areas. Furthermore, the model identified correlations between DNA feature types and production delays, providing new insights into the mechanisms of RNA synthesis delays.

Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have provided significant insights, and it's now assumed that shapes similar to that of 58Ni, which exhibits a clear proton and neutron deformation, occur in 64Ni at low spins. However, it's essential to note that the proton and neutron deformations in 64Ni may not be equally present and that certain configurations might show a more symmetrical shape. Furthermore, it's suggested that as spins increase, ground-state shapes in both 58Ni and 64Ni become similar, indicating that J-Islam factor plays a crucial role in shaping (excited) states across these nuclei.

We provide an overview of recent breakthroughs in chiral gauge theories that are non-supersymmetric. By examining various chiral theories, such as the $SU(N)$ theory with an antisymmetric bi-fundamental field, as well as the $Sp(N)$ and $SO(N)$ theories, we identify and evaluate both the holomorphic anomaly and the elliptic genus for the free theory and various Seiberg duality relations. Additionally, we explore non-supersymmetric versions of the Veneziano dualities and propose novel monopole and twist embedding techniques for dualities involving baryon vertices.

A linear complementary pair of group codes $(C, D)$ is formed when the direct sum of $C$ and $D$ results in the entire group algebra $R$. In the specific case of the quaternion algebra over a field with two elements, we identify pairs of group codes that are linear complements to each other.

We present a novel, simple summary of a function's behavior in a graphical model, expressed as a vector of brief functional insights. This explicit representation allows for the efficient resolution of complex marginally optimal problems and constrained optimization issues within graphical models, by enabling the rapid determination of a function's behavior given a change in variable configuration. Our proposed summary vector can be viewed as a functional analog to the mean-field approximation in the context of variational inference. It provides a concise, easily interpretable alternative to the direct computation of a function, which often involves computationally demanding combinatorial calculations. For instance, exactly solving the MPE problem in a directed graphical model outside of a gauge equivalence takes linear time when utilizing our proposed summary vector, whereas it requires exponential time when using standard algorithms. Additionally, this framework yields a simple, fast method for constrained optimization issues, allowing for the efficient suppression of spurious solutions that arise through approximate inference. Finally, our proposed summary vector offers a useful tool for analyzing a function's behavior in the context of its Taylor expansion, particularly when the function exhibits structural properties.

The rapid growth of automation across various industries has led to an uptick in visual disruptions, such as objects obstructing camera views, which can be resolved by utilizing computer vision. The emerging technology of multi-sensor integration has also given rise to a greater need for innovation, as seen in the rising importance of sensor fusion in robotic exploration and the burgeoning field of audio-visual integration. In this research, we address the novel problem of detecting fallen items by fusion of auditory and visual cues from a robotic platform. The proposed solution comprises an audio-based detector that identifies the type of item using the sound's frequency, and a vision-based tracker that pinpoints the item using the video footage and audio waveform's temporal connection. The effectiveness of this solution was tested in a controlled environment with human participants simulating item drops, and the results show that the combined approach outperforms a purely visual method in item recognition and tracking accuracy.

When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity, or shear thickening. This process can be slowed down by lowering the stress until the mixture's viscosity increases in a sub-linear, highly sensitive manner, or in some cases, prevents the thickening altogether, or at least delays it until an exceptionally high stress threshold is reached. Despite its widespread occurrence, the cause of this sudden and severe thickening has long been a subject of debate. In order to offer explanations for the different forms that shear thickening can take, we have created a unified theoretical framework. This framework is based on two main principles: that a sudden and severe thickening is triggered by a sudden shift in density due to the overwhelming impact of stress, and that the mixture's properties are largely determined by a repulsive force between particles, or in the case of mixtures with attractive forces, a force that is not overly strong. In our framework, the viscosity of the mixture is affected by two components, one representing rigidity and another that opposes flow, with the opposition to flow being more pronounced at lower stresses, or in some cases, an exception to viscosity being seen at low stresses. This study explores the hourly electricity consumption pattern in Bangladesh's power crisis period using the Three Parameter Mixed Skew Generalized Distribution. The model's parameters are estimated via the Expectation Maximum method and its reliability validated using Kolmogorov-Smirnov goodness-of-fit tests. The findings reveal that the TPMSGK distribution offers an excellent fit to the observed data, significantly outperforming other distributions in terms of goodness-of-fit.

An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional work has been inadequately studied is that of professional knowledge work on the Web. This study examines public sector officials' reliance on their organization's publicly accessible Google Web search settings, which can either reveal personal information or simply tailor search results based on the organization's activities. Our results show that these tailored searches significantly shape officials' information seeking and retrieval habits on the Web and, more crucially, that they can significantly reduce the range of information these experts encounter during work hours. In fact, we found that by expanding from common to unique search terms, up to 34% of relevant information on the Web may be missed due to Web search personalisation. To promote comprehensive discoveries, we suggest that public sector officials (1) utilize exploration tools beyond their organization's public Google Web search settings, (2) regularly change their search settings or use incognito mode, and (3) incorporate search field expansion techniques in their information seeking strategies.

Automatically creating code from visual representations is a crucial area of study for reducing the time and effort required in software development. Graph-based representations offer a suitable alternative to traditional flow charts for encoding program structure and enabling the development of machine learning models. Previous studies have focused on using optical character recognition and machine learning to learn program representations from these graphs. This approach is contrasted with a novel method that employs a graph convolutional neural network to directly recognize and interpret the symbolic graphs. The latter method is exemplified through its application on the classical problem of generating Perl programs from flow charts, and the results indicate that it surpasses the performance of the optical character recognition-based method while also being more efficient and straightforward. The associated toolkits and results have been made available for the convenience of the research community.

This text explores various reduction techniques employed in climate science with a focus on dynamical systems and nonlinear partial differential equations. It briefly introduces key methodologies such as the center manifold reduction, effective medium theory, homogenization, and center manifold reduction with an emphasis on their applications in climate research.

The development of kilonova ejecta through the interaction of the explosive shock with the dense, radioactive matter created in the merger has been a topic of interest in the emerging field of gravitational wave research. To gain a deeper understanding of this phenomenon, the residual ejecta of osmium and gold with an atomic number of four, formed in the r-process, are analyzed using the most up-to-date relativistic atomic theory. Our study employs the relativistic atomic model to determine the essential atomic parameters, including energy levels, wave functions, and radiation patterns. To facilitate the development of practical opacity tables, we also calculated the Gaunt factors for the s, p, and d transitions using various methods, including the dispersion theory, the relativistic Gaunt factor model, the sum rules approach, and the atomic structure calculations. Our findings reveal that the opacity of the Os-like and Au-like ions can be accurately represented by the relativistic blackbody, the radiation gas, the osmium zirconium opacity table, and the gold barium opacity table, except in the vicinity of the resonance lines. In particular, the resonance lines of Au IV and Os I, characterized by strong negative dispersion and a sharp increase in the optical cross section at specific energies, significantly affect the opacity in the ultraviolet and far-ultraviolet ranges. Moreover, to validate our results and provide a framework for future research, we compiled the extensive tables of osmium and gold opacities in the 0-340 keV energy

Deep learning-based methods are increasingly being used for the automated analysis of abdominal organs, including the gallbladder and its surroundings, in medical imaging. However, a reliable segmentation of the gastrointestinal region is often hindered by the variations in the anatomy and the presence of anomalies, such as an enlarged GB or neighboring organs' interferences. These challenges make the GI region segmentation a complex task, particularly in abdominal X-ray CT scans, which usually have low-contrast images and a complex background. In this study, we explored the effectiveness of several deep learning-based approaches for GI region segmentation using a diverse dataset of 1,000 CT scans, both with and without anomalies. The proposed solutions demonstrated exceptional accuracy, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.95 and 0.96, respectively. Notably, our best-performing model, a saliency-based approach, significantly outperformed an existing state-of-the-art method, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.04 and 0.06 improvement, respectively.

Compositional data analysis, a field of study that deals with complex datasets, undergoes significant transformation in this paper, illustrating its underlying mathematical and graphical components via linear algebra and visualization techniques. The paper also clarifies the common pitfalls in the interpretation of compositional data, offering researchers valuable guidance.

Past research has suggested that sub-Saturn mass planet formation encounters difficulties when born in metal-poor environments and retaining volatile materials during the planetary formation process.  To further explore this theory, the CORALIE/HARPS radial velocity survey was conducted over the period of 1998-2018, aiming to identify Volatile-Rich Planets (VRPs) with masses between those of Neptune and Uranus.  Using the established VRP criterion of log(Q$_{2-10}$ $<$$-0.53$ based on model-predicted volatile enrichment, the analysis identified 14 planets out of 366 candidates, all with masses below 5 $M_{\earth}$ that fit the required mass range and had up to 3 significant $\beta$-index values, indicating gravitational influence from multiple planets.  Furthermore, the analysis compared planet masses and orbital periods to theoretical planetary boundaries, showing that 9 out of 14 planets lie within the proposed "No Man's Land" where planet formation is thought to be challenging.  Using a simulation-based approach to assess the statistical significance of these results against a broader sampling of planetary data, the analysis found no substantial evidence supporting the concept of 'No Man's Land' where sub-Saturn mass planets are expected to lack existence.

In the field of autonomous systems, the way a robot pays attention to its environment is critical to its ability to adapt and make decisions, yet it can be easily disrupted by uncertain information. This study focuses on improving a robot's ability to adapt to changing situations by paying close attention to the relationships between different parts of its environment. The researchers developed a new approach that helps the robot focus on the most useful information and makes it easier for it to operate even when surrounded by uncertainty. This approach is based on the idea that a well-performing robot should be able to accurately predict the information it receives from its sensors by looking at the world around it. To achieve this, the researchers used a training method that encourages the robot to focus on the relationships between its sensors and the environment. The results show that this approach is successful in a simulation that models a robot's ability to collect information in a dynamic and constantly changing environment.

Our research centers around compressed dark matter scenarios, specifically within
Yukawa-type systems consisting of one compressed baryon and one antibaryon.
By incorporating Dirac fermions to mediate the interaction, the model is
mathematically self-consistent and possesses a Meissner effect, analogous to
high-temperature superconductivity. The mechanism of the interaction is
governed by the exchange of fermions, and we demonstrate that the Compton
wavefunction of the dark matter particles is non-zero, implying a finite
charge. The analysis further reveals that the Yukawa interaction is
physically
distinct from other types of forces, such as gravitational or electromagnetic
dualities. Last but not least, we examine the potential for the Yukawa
interaction to be detected through laboratory-based searches.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) can efficiently solve complex problems that demand memory, error correction, and control over sequential activities. Despite their potential, standard RNNs often require extensive training and, therefore, significant time. In contrast, biological brain networks, which are thought to be recurrent in nature, typically operate within limited time frames even though their underlying mechanisms are not clearly understood. This study aims to uncover the secrets of biological inspiration by investigating the capabilities of simple, efficiently-trained sparse RNNs in addressing a range of cognitive tasks. We demonstrate that these sparse RNNs can learn quickly and perform well on a variety of tasks, including navigation, control of dynamic systems, prediction, and more. We further show that their structure, although initially randomly generated, often adapts to resemble functional brain networks, which are characterized by localized and interconnected components. This study confirms that the concept of the 'lottery ticket theorem' can be applied to cognitive neuroscience, giving rise to new avenues for research that combines neural networks with the study of brain function.

We provide a comprehensive classification of 8-dimensional nilpotent algebras along with their dimensions, and comment on the associated dimensions. Moreover, we offer an online database for the algebras in this classification, which can be accessed via MATHEMATICA. Using this database, we develop an interactive tool to visualize the categorization of nilpotent algebras in terms of their dimensions.

Active galactic nuclei with exceptionally powerful radio signals are among the brightest known celestial sources, spanning across a wide range of wavelengths. These powerful jets from supermassive black holes can significantly impact surrounding gas and dust within and outside the accretion disk. In this study, we explore how these cosmic objects influence their environment, particularly at the highest observed redshifts, influenced by the cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation. We examined the effects of CMB on the growth of black holes and the emission of relativistic particles within jets through numerical simulations. For the most extreme AGNs at redshifts above 6.5, the CMB's influence leads to decreased growth rates of the black holes, primarily driven by particles losing energy and being ejected from the accretion disk rather than particles within the jets. This suggests CMB radiation can slow down the growth of the black holes most active at the highest observed redshifts, potentially affecting the evolution of the universe and the formation of these cosmic objects.

The general relativity framework assumes the presence of a spacetime metric, with matter and gravity both described through its variations. However, a particular theoretical form of gravity, referred to as "non-cinetic gravity," postulates that the metric itself, rather than its tensor version, constitutes the gravitational field, thereby necessitating an explicit representation, or Lagrangian, to describe this type of gravity. Our study aims to explore the Lagrangian formulation for non-cinetic gravity, building upon our previous findings regarding the appropriate Hamiltonian formulation for this theory, as determined by our previous publication.

This study presents an enhanced approach to 3D image features that incorporates invariance to discrete symmetry by considering inversions of spatial axes and image contrast.  The proposed descriptor includes a binary feature that distinguishes between the sign of the Laplacian operator's results, making it immune to image inversion and 3D transformations that reverse spatial coordinates, achieving SP-symmetry or SP-invariance. This generalization of symmetry applies to arbitrary scalar image fields and encompasses well-known CP-symmetry seen in charged elementary particles. Local feature orientation is represented as a set of independent states accounting for possible reflections, irrespective of image intensity inversion. Two key axis vectors are derived from observed image data, along with a third axial vector defined by the right-hand rule. Adding the sign component to the traditional geometry of local features (location, scale, orientation) generates descriptors that are robust to coordinate and intensity inversions. These enhanced feature properties are integrated into symmetric kernel-based point-wise registration, modeled using binary feature correspondence. Empirical results obtained from experiments using the CPD algorithm demonstrate the high precision and speed of the SIFT-CPD kernels in image registration, particularly for complex datasets such as human brains, CT scans, and MRI images, even when they exhibit variations in intensity, occlusions, or abnormal growths like tumors. This approach provides invariance to global scale, rotation, translation, and input data intensity inversions.

We've analyzed the sightlines and orbital arrangements of double-degenerate binary systems that comprise white dwarfs in close proximity to each other, utilizing data from various photometric and spectroscopic observations in total. Our in-depth examination of the system SDSS J082239.54+304857.19 has uncovered detailed patterns and characteristics in the stars' behavioral patterns in the stars' movements around each other, both in terms of their overall 40.5-minute orbital cycle and individual grid-patterned grid-like patterns occurring at the same site. The study also reveals that the system likely exhibits a somewhat tilted orbital plane that is viewed nearly directly from Earth.
