The analysis further indicates that the smaller of the two white dwarfs in the system has a diameter equivalent to about 11.9 Martian diameters and the estimated masses for the stars are roughly in the range of 0.95 to 1.05 solar masses. The observed and analyzed data from the system have allowed for the accurate determination of the system's various orbital parameters, further aiding in the continued study and monitoring of the system.

In many machine learning models, global pooling layers simplify feature maps into a single vector. A commonly used technique, pooling, was initially inspired by optimal transport theory, where it can be equated with solving the OT problem using uniform weights within each feature map. Nonetheless, practical global pooling layers in models often diverge from this ideal, resulting in suboptimal performance. This study explores these deviations and proposes a new, theoretically grounded global pooling layer based on OT principles, enhancing the standard methods currently used in models. The findings demonstrate that the novel approach surpasses the existing techniques in both 2D and 3D image classification tasks.

The primary goal of this research is to examine aspects of the validity of the active galactic nucleus unification theory. Our study focused on three specific aspects: the host galaxy types, the spatial orientations, and the relative power ratios between the central black hole and the host galaxy, all with a focus on different Hubble types. To this end, we conducted a detailed visual inspection of 432 southern active galactic nuclei (AGN), and obtained useful data for 312 of these sources. During our visual inspection, we relied on digitized galaxy cores from the Second Revised AFGL (RAFGL2) Catalog to determine the host galaxies and obtained spatial orientations from the Digitized Second Southern Sky Catalog. Using our collected data, we created plots to compare the distribution of galaxy types and orientations, as well as the relationship between the central brightness and the host galaxy brightness, all while distinguishing between different Hubble types and orientation classes. Furthermore, we conducted statistical analyses using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov method to assess whether the distributions of galaxy types and orientations are significantly different. Our key findings include the presence of Hubble type differences, the same range of galaxy orientations for AGN of various types, and evidence suggesting that LINERs and Seyfert 2 Galaxies have a different relationship between the central brightness and the host galaxy brightness.

This paper delves into a comprehensive analysis of general rotational surfaces in the 4-dimensional Euclidean space, focusing on flat general rotation surfaces characterized by a 1-type Gaussian map. Additionally, it's established that a non-planar, flat general rotation surface with this distinct Gaussian map feature is a Lie group if and only if it's a Clifford torus.

Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires significant effort,
so many researchers opt for pre-training their model on a different task before
further refining it using a labeled dataset. Mega-resolution image
classification has been a common choice, but we investigate whether depth
estimation can serve as a better pre-training task in this study. Our key
findings are as follows: (1) Depth estimation can enhance downstream segmentation
results, but only when the pre-trained model is fine-tuned; (2) On the other
hand, when the pre-trained weights are fixed, mega-resolution image
classification yields superior outcomes; (3) Despite these observations, we
demonstrate that the enhanced performance resulting from depth estimation can be
replicated by incorporating an external depth predictor into the neural
network and adjusting the optimizer accordingly.

The increasing availability of time-series data from various sources, both formal and informal, presents an opportunity for developing systems that can create natural, human-like descriptions of time-series data, such as weather forecasts and medical reports. Current approaches to narrating time-series data are often tied to specific domains and require substantial training on data with correctly formatted labels. To address this limitation, we present TCube, a novel system that can automatically create high-quality, readable descriptions for given time-series data without requiring domain-specific knowledge. TCube uses a novel, domain-agnostic method to select significant time-series segments and employs a neural transformer to generate descriptions in a choice of simple or detailed styles. Our experimental results demonstrate that TCube surpasses state-of-the-art models in both accuracy and fluency, with a particular advantage in reducing the risk of incorrect time-series segment interpretations. Additionally, TCube shows great promise in creating natural descriptions for real-world scenarios, such as providing human-in-the-loop corrections and producing descriptions from raw sensory data.

The ATLAS experiment has made key observations in studies of beauty mesons. Notably, the experiment has detected a notable difference in how certain processes occur when produced by particles of different charges, a difference that does not follow the standard theory. The observation of a rare occurrence, in which a particle decays in a particular way, but with opposite properties, has also been made. Furthermore, the experiment has measured a rare occurrence in another particle and found it to occur more frequently than predicted by the standard theory. The experiment has also measured branching ratios - or probabilities of occurrence - for two separate events involving different particles.

On a Cayley tree, we examine the Ising model and find novel periodic and antiperiodic configurations that act as thermodynamic limits, alongside the standard ferromagnetic and paramagnetic states. These novel configurations exhibit unique, 2-stage periodic patterns.

This study explores the global well-posedness of solutions to certain first-order hyperbolic equations with coefficients dependent on $\log$ or $\sqrt{\ln}$ terms, acting as principles in space variables, and establishes the global existence of smooth solutions. Notably, these principles can be considered sublogarithmic, providing a broader framework for understanding the behavior of such equations. The methods employed involve the construction of a microlocal wavefront location variable, allowing for the application of an invariant metric tensor and a specific type of Carleman estimate, ultimately leading to the establishment of an observable operator. The results can be extended to cover certain quasilinear equations with smooth coefficients and additional lower-order terms.

This research introduces a novel application of the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network to tackle the challenging task of Japanese term segmentation. Building on previous breakthroughs in Chinese term segmentation using LSTM and Bidirectional LSTM, this study adapts LSTM and its variants for the more complex Japanese language, incorporating the necessary character encoding to account for multiple base forms. Evaluations on previously established datasets demonstrate that Bidirectional LSTM and LSTM with character embeddings achieve higher accuracy than existing state-of-the-art methods, showcasing the efficacy of LSTM in addressing the intricacies of Japanese term segmentation.

External web links on Stack Overflow can significantly enhance the coding experience for developers by providing access to useful information from outside the platform. To investigate the benefits of these links, we conducted a study on the most frequently shared external sources commonly referenced by SO users. Our analysis involved reviewing the top-related tags associated with the 10 million+ SO questions that included an external web link. Among the links shared, we found that YouTube, GitHub, and Bitbucket were among the popular platforms referenced by users. Our findings also showed that SO users frequently share external sources related to coding tools, libraries, and other programming resources, highlighting the utility of these links in supporting on-platform discussions.

Galactic rotation curves show a range of varying inner slopes. Observations suggest a potential relationship between a galaxy's brightness and its central dark matter, indicating the need for a more comprehensive explanation. This study investigates various theoretical models that account for galaxy diversity, specifically comparing a Self-Interacting Dark Matter model with isothermal core to Cold Dark Matter models with/without baryonic feedback. To evaluate these models, fit metrics are used to assess their effectiveness in reproducing observed rotation curves. To be considered, a model must meet a reliability criterion in its fit. The top contenders include the $\Lambda$CDM models with proper sampling of initial conditions and a high resolution for small-scale simulations, as well as a Special Relativity Quantum Field Theory model. An effective Lambda-CDM model requires higher resolution for the central region of the galaxy, allowing it to accurately reproduce observed rotation curves. On the other hand, a Quantum Field Theory model, derived from its relativistic counterpart, provides a consistent fit to observed data, offering a unified explanation for both large and small-scale phenomena.

To combat climate change, nations must collaborate on a global scale, 
executing and sustaining agreements such as the Paris Accord.
The new climate change agreements necessitate frequent and productive 
international negotiations among countries.
Climate research studies often uncover compelling reasons to take 
environmental action, yet, they frequently fail to translate into 
government policy due to the complex process of international 
negotiations and information dissemination.
We propose the creation of a Climate Knowledge Base, a comprehensive 
database combining structured and unstructured data, integrated with dynamic 
geospatial mapping tools, to facilitate climate discussion and analysis.
Our knowledge base addresses critical challenges of climate negotiation 
information gaps by providing a framework for data analysis and 
interpretation, as demonstrated in our initial results.
We also present ClimateNet, an innovative network visualization 
component, enabling effective climate negotiation resolution by illustrating 
country-level negotiation priorities and their geo-spatial context.
Moreover, ClimateNet enhances the understanding of negotiation 
strategies through analysis of country-specific priorities and their relation 
to surrounding nations and environmental features.

Clinical data, particularly clinical notes, offer valuable information on patient symptoms, but due to disparities in data collection and representation, models trained on one dataset often struggle to perform accurately on another due to the inherent domain shifts. To address this challenge, researchers suggest using Domain Generalization to produce a single, universal model that can adapt to various domains. This study specifically focuses on extracting symptoms from clinical notes across different domains and proposes an innovative pre-training strategy known as Symptom Signal Pre-Training (SPT) to enhance the performance of Universal Models. By utilizing unlabeled notes from multiple domains, the SPT strategy trains the model to recognize key symptoms more effectively. To evaluate the effectiveness of this approach, the researchers conducted comprehensive experiments on two widely-used real-world datasets: Clinical Question Answering and Joint Disease and Symptom Extraction, demonstrating substantial improvements over baseline models and current state-of-the-art techniques. Notably, the results show that the SPT strategy yields a 9.2% enhancement in performance over the next best method, offering significant practical value in developing more versatile and adaptable clinical symptom extraction models.

Deep reinforcement learning strategies have gained significant attention in the field of autonomous driving due to their ability to guide virtual self-driving cars without the need for extensive map data. A popular choice for autonomous driving, DRL has shown success in a variety of tasks, such as following a target, avoiding collisions, and navigating through complex environments. A common approach for training DRL agents is DDPG, which builds upon the maximum entropy principle from RL. In our submission, we provide a re-implemented version of the DRL agent based on DDPG, alongside the corresponding rewards function. This rewards function is designed to penalize the agent for deviating from the lane or colliding with other objects, while encouraging it to follow a target vehicle or waypoint. Additionally, we include an auxiliary task rewards function to promote the agent's forward progression. We then combine this rewards function with an auxiliary task rewards function to guide the agent towards a stochastic trajectory that better utilizes the information available during training. Notably, our method does not incorporate the use of an adversarial generative model, instead leveraging the DRL agent to explore and dissect the underlying dynamics of the autonomous driving task. This is evident in our experiment where we compare our approach with an alternative method that omits the auxiliary task, yielding a positive impact on DRL agent's performance. Furthermore, our results demonstrate the efficacy of our rewards function in facilitating a seamless transition to a real-world driving scenario.

In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. We present a proposal to utilize a Random Neural Network as a versatile classifying model that combines the efficiency of spiking neural networks with the high classification accuracy achieved by traditional neural networks, showcasing this concept's efficacy across real-world classification datasets.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark stars under the influence of a magnetic field at finite temperature, employing a MIT-bags model. The energy density, entropy, and pressure of the quark clusters are calculated in terms of the bag constant and strange quark chemical potential, and are further analyzed in relation to temperature and spin polarization. Additionally, equations for electric and magnetic potentials are developed in the presence of a magnetic field, and a proposed solution for the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars that maintains overall stability is presented.

Pando, an innovative project, seeks to establish a breakthrough in Computational Self-Expression, a concept pioneered by David R. Olson. Pando creates an innovative system that enables users to create dynamic, interactive stories, comparable to Hypertext Fiction, yet accessible through browsers, powered by JavaScript, without requiring prior coding knowledge. Furthermore, Pando's stories can be viewed as multimedia presentations, combining text, images, and video, controlled by a user-defined timeline. Currently, Pando supports a wide range of storytelling features, including serial narratives, branched stories, and even video-based documentaries. To facilitate creativity, Pando offers a comprehensive set of tutorials and a responsive development environment, enabling seamless authoring, testing, and publication of stories.

This research develops novel nonparametric estimation techniques for nonlinear eigenproblems under both fixed and evolving dimension scenarios. We introduce an estimators based on minimal rational interpolation for the eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors of a nonlinear operator $\mathcal{T}$. The study covers a broad spectrum of operators, including matrices with entries linked to functions that exhibit smooth dependencies and operators defined by summations of smooth functions. The estimation approach leverages an operator approximation $\widehat{\mathcal{H}}$ based on observations of the operator's iterations, applied to an initial test function. The study demonstrates that these estimators are exceptionally efficient in a variety of situations and, in the case of evolving dimensions, are optimal among a particular class of estimators. The results can be applied to estimate nonlinear eigenfunctions in diverse applications such as functional data analysis, statistical mechanics, and quantum chemistry, assuming access to noisy samples of the operator's iterations.

We establish a connection between intermediate beta transforms and a type of greedy beta transform that excludes a specific interval. This relationship enables us to derive new insights from earlier studies on beta transforms, as well as establish novel results that weren't addressed by those studies. For instance, we can determine the specific orbit parameters for certain points in this context, even though this might not be possible in all cases, as illustrated by counterexamples.

We've found that gauge theories with $SO(N_{c})$ as a gauge group and fundamental fermions of both chiralities can form in a way that shows confinement, where the fermions are held together in a way that can't be broken down, and where the theory becomes very complicated at low energies. By using a $1/N$ expansion and developing an analogy with a geometric structure called a 'wall', we've been able to prove that these properties hold rigorously, making our findings a true confinement in a rigorous sense. Unlike theories with $SU(N_{c})$ as a gauge group, the properties of these theories have remained a mystery for 40 years, even in relation to common theories such as QCD.

Machine learning models such as random forests and boosted trees achieve high accuracy but have difficulty being understood, making them hard to use in a 'what if' scenario. A new method called Disentangled Attribution Curves (DAC) helps to explain the behavior of these models by highlighting the key variables that most affect the prediction, and showing the relative influence of each variable. This means that even if a variable is not the most influential, it can still have an impact on the prediction if it is part of a more complex feature set. DAC works by reversing the training of the model and using an optimization technique to find the variables most responsible for the prediction, and has been tested on variables that were known in advance as well as those that were not.

Federated Learning seeks to train accurate machine learning models while maintaining user privacy by performing calculations on local devices and averaging the updates. Despite this, the server where updates are aggregated has access to the training data, which can be seen as a violation of user privacy. To address this issue, we propose an innovative approach called Flatee, integrating Remote Procedure Call based Trusted Execution Environments and Secret Sharing to protect data and aggregation operations in both Federated Learning and Vertical Federated Learning.

Self-driving vehicle software demands significant computational power, 
approximately equivalent to that required by a high-end graphics GPU. 
Although significant, this requirement still presents an opportunity for 
miniaturization to embedded systems, which could greatly expand their use 
in autonomous vehicles, improving safety through redundant system operation. 
To fully utilize this miniaturization, it is crucial to optimize and tailor
 autonomous driving functions specifically for the capabilities of embedded systems. 
This paper explores the optimization of deep learning-based driver behavior 
prediction and evaluates the efficiency of various models on embedded devices.

This paper introduces a new approach called Timeloops that enables the autonomous learning of system call filters for individual microservices during runtime, without requiring manual intervention. By utilizing a dynamic memory structure, Timeloops constructs a training dataset of known system calls for each microservice and learns to combine these calls with a Timetable, a novel filter mechanism analogous to vector masks, to grant or deny access to specific system calls at predetermined times. This methodology leverages the containerized design of microservices to efficiently optimize system call filters. Furthermore, Timeloops's learning capabilities allow it to adapt to changes such as system updates or malicious activity, using a combination of offline and online model updating techniques. We have successfully implemented Timeloops on top of the Linux kernel and evaluated its effectiveness by simulating various security scenarios, revealing that it can learn highly accurate system call filters and rapidly adapt to significant security breaches, all while enhancing system performance and reducing complexity.

Merchandise space forms provide a useful framework for managing complex decision-making processes by representing items as vectors in a high-dimensional space. To take advantage of this framework, it is essential to develop effective classifiers that can distinguish between items with desirable and undesirable characteristics in this space. To that end, this paper explores the theoretical basis for linear classification in merchandise space forms and presents a new classification method, enhancing the existing literature's limited set of tools. Furthermore, a comprehensive computational study evaluates the performance of this proposed method using data from a real-world retail environment, demonstrating its benefits through actionable insights and an observable increase in sales.

We revisit the stellar environment surrounding a supermassive black hole using the $N$-body simulation "Symbiotic". This simulation re-establishes the established stellar distribution patterns, 'Arches', 'Pfleiderer', and 'Outer Arches', within the strong separation regime. It also reveals new findings: The 'Arches' pattern persists even when considering stochastic acceleration taking into account the overall potential. The simulation also confirms that the 'Arches' and 'Pfleiderer' patterns merge at about three orbital periods. Although 'Pfleiderer' components appear to show circularization over millions of years, they actually maintain their initial orbital properties. The presence of stellar masses greater than eight solar masses has little impact on the environment. Consequently, even extremely massive black holes with variable accretion rates still exhibit comparable stellar distributions as those predicted for steady-state scenarios.

This functions as a foundational tutorial at the 2018 European Control Conference, delivering a clear modeling approach for designing Random Model Predictive Controllers (RMPCs). A flexible, compact modeling framework is offered that covers:
 1. System observation under uncertainty: modeling as an iterative, probabilistic observation process.
 2. Control strategies: defining them as sequential, probabilistic actions.
3. Optimization within a predictive framework: formulating an optimization problem that incorporates past observations and future predictions to determine the best course of action.
A series of simulations demonstrate how to design an RMPC for a basic swing-up-and-capture problem on a pendulum, highlighting the trade-offs between performance and constraints.

This paper presents a novel approach to extract key elements from large datasets by applying a set of carefully designed linear measurements. These measurements are further reduced to obtain the most influential components from the data, while ensuring the retention of essential information. Our method is inspired by Singular Component Analysis and is a concise extension of Compressive Sensing to multi-dimensional data analysis. We provide theoretical foundations for its success and introduce an efficient solution strategy to minimize the number of measurements required. To recover the original data and components efficiently, we propose a series of algorithms combining optimization and reconstruction techniques. Our numerical results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach and showcase its superiority over traditional methods in large datasets.

To analyze the interplay of species competition and colonization dynamics, we introduce an electoral model that uses a set of rules mimicking a democratic process. This model is based on a lattice geometry where a species' ability to win elections is influenced by its current population and colonization success. We find that the model exhibits various species interactions, including exclusive, competitive, and cooperative behaviors, which are a consequence of the tradeoff between species competition and colonization. The model shows two main transitions, one being arbitrary and the other influenced by noise levels. The model's behavior doesn't match the predictions of the fundamental models of species interactions, indicating that its complex rule set leads to diverse patterns of species exclusion and coexistence.

We study the collection of local von Neumann algebras within abelian quantum double models. For a compact Riemann surface, the intersection of local von Neumann algebras associated with distinct partitions is abelian, resulting in a monoidal category whose unit is the von Neumann algebra on compact rectangles. The functors that extend to the larger collection of von Neumann algebras on the surface are unique up to a scalar multiple.

To enhance magnon-photon-phonon entanglement in cavity magnomechanics, we develop an approach incorporating a comprehensive quantum model incorporating the effects of phonon phasing and position, magnon phasing and position, and photon exchange. We utilize the Kimura effect and implement a coherent feedback mechanism to optimize entanglement. Our results indicate that the steady-state entanglement among the system's components can be significantly improved with the inclusion of this coherent feedback process. Moreover, we find that the local entanglement among the magnon, photon, and phonon can be maintained and even preserved in the long-term, attributing this stability to the coherent feedback loop.

We have single-handedly published a comprehensive collection of single-color, single-polarized triple-collinear splitting operators at the one-loop level within a dimensionally-controlled QCD framework. These operators were initially derived using effective field theory methods and then further detailed with an emphasis on their behavior in dimensions other than four. Additionally, we have provided an explanation of how double and triple collinear operators are connected through an evolution equation, which highlights their role in process descriptions at different scales. These operators hold significant importance in understanding multi-partonic processes and allow for a scale-based explanation of cross-sections and asymmetries.

To expand the Cohen-Macaulayification procedure, we have formulated an expanded version of Neron desingularization, applicable to one-dimensional local rings, and have successfully implemented it through a sequence of finite, computationally manageable steps.

The country's largest collection of sundials is housed at the Indonesian National Museum, featuring over 500 items spanning centuries to date. These sundial artifacts hold significant scientific value in understanding ancient cultures and technological advancements. However, the failure to conduct thorough research on these artifacts results in the lack of detailed data on the collection. Therefore, the primary objective of the proposed project, titled Suryakala-Nusantara, is to document and study the collection through a comprehensive database and scientific analysis of its spatial and temporal aspects. The project will also develop educational materials for children and adults to raise awareness about sundials as a valuable tool in understanding astronomy and history.

In an integrated data and energy networking system, a cognitive reflecting surface is utilized to address interference within local area networks, extending to device-to-device communications and wireless power transfer. The reflecting surface's filtering vector is treated as a controllable variable to minimize the owner's data traffic cost while ensuring the other devices' power transfer costs and their own power in doing so. The problem is a non-convex multi-mMO, multi-user system, for which we present a successive convex approximation algorithm combined with a low-complexity heuristic as efficient alternatives. The proposed schemes are shown to achieve a comparable performance to the optimal method, with significantly reduced computational requirements.

The widespread use of LDV technology, crucial in analyzing and understanding complex flows, has led to significant interest in implementing it for studying two-dimensional velocity distributions in real-time, essential in developing and optimizing industrial systems, as well as acquiring detailed data for in-depth research purposes. This interest has given rise to a technique called "distant operation" of an LDV system, allowing the acquisition of two-dimensional velocity data by moving the measurement point in a controlled manner, automating the data collection process, and making it possible to conduct extensive research without extensive personnel costs. This paper aims to introduce the distant operation method, presenting the results of its application to a free jet scenario.

This note revisits questions regarding the expressiveness of first-order logic with binary relations, specifically addressing a query posed in a previous paper (Bullig, Kihara, and Künzel 2022). We resolve this inquiry by demonstrating that the proposed characterization is indeed correct, with an accompanying proof.

Programmable phase plates (PPhPs) have emerged as vital tools for enhancing contrast in transmission electron microscopy (TEM), particularly for imaging fragile and sensitive specimens. Unlike conventional phase plates, which are fixed, PPhPs can be dynamically adjusted to accommodate various specimen types. This level of flexibility has prompted researchers to explore the possibility of using PPhPs as error correctors in TEM to mitigate imaging distortions. In this work, the potential of PPhPs acting as aberration correctors is investigated using computational methods. Our findings suggest that, in practice, PPhPs are unable to effectively correct all types of aberrations, particularly those with high spatial frequencies. Therefore, we advise against utilizing PPhPs as aberration correctors, as their primary strength lies in enhancing contrast, not correcting distortions.

This research focuses on evaluating binary choices and investigating how their assessment affects decision-making processes in situations involving uncertainty. It reveals that individuals' risk-taking behaviors are often driven by an tendency to overvalue rare outcomes (as depicted in Figure 1) rather than a failure to consider all possible consequences (as depicted in Figure 2). Furthermore, we demonstrate that accounting for a limited set of probabilistic assessment errors does not address the issue of leptokurtic risk-taking (as shown in Figure 3), thereby undermining the utility of assessment-based approaches in modeling such behavior.

This study establishes a precise formula for calculating the probability distribution of the distance from a random walk's origin in a d-dimensional integer space, with a given step size of $s$, and a positive integer value of $n$. The proposed formula is validated through both mathematical proof and numerical modeling, with the associated computation time discussed.

Our investigation involves a detailed examination, aided by numerical methods, of the tensor type GOP singularity, a type of polymer black hole singularity, in three distinct spacetime dimensions. This analysis is complemented by theoretical findings regarding the quasinormal modes of the GO-P pullin type black hole, a hyperbolic type, which we have also numerically verified. The transition from the polymer type G-O-P singularity to a finite, non-zero radius, known as the Cecotti-Gregory type, is also explored.

We have performed a study on the thermal screening and heat capacity of graphene sheets with various types of doping, using a self-consistent electronic-phonon interaction approach at finite temperatures. The analysis focuses on the effect of temperature on the electronic and phononic properties of graphene. For half-filled graphene, our results show that the thermal screening length is largely determined by the plasmon energy and the sound speeds of the two graphene phonon modes. The integration of the Fermi-Dirac distribution and the phonon occupation factor in the self-consistent equations allows us to include the electronic and phononic excitations in the screening potential at finite temperatures. In addition, our numerical results for the heat capacity of doped graphene reveal that the inclusion of electronic and phononic interactions significantly modifies the Berezin-Shubin and Rustagi formulas, particularly at high temperatures where the Fermi functions and phonon occupation factor deviate from their 0K behavior. The analysis also highlights the distinct contributions of the three graphene valleys to the heat capacity, pointing out that these valley contributions should be considered for accurate calculations of the heat capacity at high temperatures and moderate doping levels. Finally, our heat capacity results are comparable to each other and to existing experiments on graphene, providing a valuable basis for the interpretation of future experiments.

This research introduces Context-aware Speech Production (CAP), a model that generates spoken language based on its semantic meaning. To achieve this, CAP uses a novel, context-specific masking technique to select relevant speech features. By doing so, it ensures the produced speech meets the desired semantic requirements. For instance, when the meaning includes the phrase "I am excited," the model will choose a prosody that fits this emotion by masking parts of the speech that don't align with it. We implement CAP by integrating a masking module into SpeechProduction, a proven speech production model. Our results show that this new approach substantially improves the naturalness of the spoken output.

We've developed a novel statistical framework, known as projected estimation, that allows us.g to make inferences about certain parameters using a non-parametric approach. We've derived an efficient method for projecting predictive estimation into a lower-dimensional space. This method maintains the same optimal properties as traditional projected estimation while providing a significant reduction in computational complexity, making it feasible for large-scale applications. We've further developed an approximation technique to extend the projection technique beyond the current boundary, enabling it to work within a broader range of confidence intervals. We've detailed the mathematical justifications behind these innovations as well as illustrated our approach through simulations and a specific case study.

Interpreting and utilizing machine learning-based predictive outputs in the face of external influences remains intricate. A potential threat against machine learning is the Man-in-the-Middle (MIM) attack, which involves manipulating communication through the transmission of crafted data without detecting the original data sent. Given that machine learning classifiers receive input data through networks, they are susceptible to MIM attacks involving malicious data and adversarial examples. To complicate this, the sender and receiver in this scenario only become aware of the attack when the machine learning model itself detects anomalies in the data received. A recent study explored how Generative Neural Networks could be used to execute MIM attacks against machine learning, with a specific focus on the SAE and LENet classifiers using the MNIST dataset. To protect machine learning models from MIM attacks, a new detection system is proposed, which relies on the use of an adaptive robust regression analyzer to detect anomalies in the data received and thereby identify MIM attacks. A series of computational experiments were carried out to evaluate the effectiveness of this solution, comparing it to the current approaches that rely on the measurement of statistical dependence and anomaly detection, which were found to be ineffective in this case.

Facebook users who accepted the invitation to join the group "Climate Change
Denial" were studied in terms of their posted content. The investigation found
that members of this group consistently adhere to a set of fixed views rejecting
climate change. The analysis of posts from 2017 to 2022 showed that group
members promoted theories claiming that climate change is a fabricated idea
spread by those who control the media. These theories vary from the notion that
it's a natural climate fluctuation to the idea that it's a hoax perpetrated by
power-hungry scientists. The consistency of these views supports the theory
that online groups spread disinformation to counteract accepted scientific
consensus.

A study focusing on the production of dark matter in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV has been carried out using the CMS detector. This study analyzed a dataset of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of collisions. It differs from earlier studies which focused on dark matter creation accompanied by a top quark pair by also considering single top quark production for comparison. Two models, one involving dark matter made by a top quark alone and another by a top quark pair through an extra heavy particle, were compared to the measurements. This study ruled out a particular region of the parameter space which was previously considered to be valid. This study's limits on the parameter space are the most stringent so far.

Given a finite category $\mathcal{C}$ of rank $n$, we establish that its derived category $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{C})$ satisfies Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality. This duality holds true for the full subcategory consisting of $n$-extranged objects in $\mathcal{C}$. Our proof leverages the theory of $n$-extranged objects, which can be seen as a category-theoretic extension of the concept of finiteness. This duality has far-reaching implications, enabling the derivation of a Galois covering functor in the context of linear species and its relationship with species of finite linear complexity.

Building upon the theory of rank-dependent social welfare functions introduced by Nitzan (2022), this research expands the framework to accommodate rank-dependent methods for analyzing complex data, including treatment effects in fields of study with potential non-Linear relationships. To illustrate the application of this framework, a novel identification strategy for the instrumental variables model with unordered interventions is proposed, along with an empirical analysis of the economic returns on different university majors using a rank-dependent model.

To advance our understanding of matter's building blocks and their interactions, future experiments necessitate the precise measurement of numerous rare and exotic particles at various energy scales. To achieve this goal, researchers propose two cutting-edge projects: the $v$-matter experiment (a high-energy anti-neutron beam facility) and PHENIx, which involves reusing the J-PANDA silicon tracker in a high-intensity $v$-production facility. Both projects aim to exploit the high-energy antiparticle beams generated by particle accelerators to study rare phenomena and increase our knowledge of the Standard Model. Specifically, the $v$-matter experiment could lead to groundbreaking discoveries in nuclear physics, while PHENIx is expected to produce a wide range of exotic hadrons and hyperons.

Most of a multiple star system's final mass is accumulated during the first few million years of its existence, specifically during the protostellar and protoplanetary phases.  To better understand the characteristics of these systems, researchers have been studying the accretion processes within a new set of complex systems consisting of a multiple star system combined with a disc.  Using advanced computer simulations, the team calculated the flow of material towards the planets and the disc's evolution over time.  Interestingly, the team Discovered that the presence of a wide binary nearby has a significant effect on the accretion rate and the shape of the stream of material feeding from the disc to the third planet in the system.  This could potentially impact the formation of planets in these complex systems, especially by affecting the amount of material accretion and the time frame in which it occurs.

This manuscript examines flat cosmological models inherent to lattice patterns for spatial geometry, with a focus on the asymptotic behavior of these models as time advances. By leveraging the symmetry of lattice patterns, we are able to pinpoint distinct cosmological models, followed by a proof that these models result in either spatially homogeneous and isotropic Milne universes or universes experiencing a Big Rip phenomenon. Our findings are further supported by an analysis of the scalar field dynamics present in the universes, with a summary of our findings presented in the conclusion.

This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model, combining the techniques of image restoration and image segmentation, to tackle the issues of leakage and mode overlapping often encountered in traditional image segmentation methods. The proposed model integrates the classical Mumford-Shah segmentations equations with an image gradient-based loss term to optimize a hidden image, ultimately resulting in cleaner segmentation outcomes. The efficiency of this approach was demonstrated through applications to both artificial and real-world images.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole properties through observations of the star's spin motion, as the spin affects the motion's pattern. The spin of heavy quasars, characterized by high luminosity, can be determined by analyzing the properties of the surrounding emission lines to derive the black hole mass, spin, and ultralight boson field parameters. We have found that, in order for the boson cloud to stabilize via a equilibrium state, the black hole's spin must be below a certain threshold; otherwise, the cloud would collapse and cause the energy released through superradiance to exceed the observed luminosity of the quasars. This leads to a possibility of setting a maximum limit on a hypothetical ultralight boson's mass, as the spin of heavy quasars could serve as a means to discover such particles.

Creating intelligent, neuroinspired systems poses a significant challenge due to its underlying hardware complexities. To overcome these challenges, a thorough comprehension of its fundamental building blocks is essential, coupled with the development of straightforward and effective prototyping tools. To address this issue, an open-source emulator was designed, utilizing the Clyde simulator and adhering to the standards of the OpenSNN project. This emulator successfully replicated the behavior of specialized neuromorphic chips, yielding accurate results within the specified time constraints. Furthermore, its performance was validated through the successful emulation of a thousand neurons and neural layers. Additionally, this emulator was successfully put to the test in a real-world application, where it accurately predict the outcomes of complex neural networks trained on a well-known dataset.

Observations of a complex noise storm in AR 12112 on May 9-10, 2012, from SDO/BFI, reveal the presence of multiple solar sources associated with a highly dynamic magnetic field. The data show how the properties of these sources and their connections undergo significant changes, with new sub-sources emerging and others disappearing as the magnetic field evolves. The sources, identified as the hot and bright plasma associated with a complex interwoven feedback loop of fine threads and fibrils, exhibit the characteristics of a long-lived and dynamic magnetic structure. The data indicate the presence of a cascade effect where the energy is distributed down the interconnecting branches of the magnetic field, causing the sources to move and interact in a complex manner. The discovery of a complex and highly dynamic magnetic structure provides the opportunity to study the underlying dynamics of the solar atmosphere through the perspective of a linked and evolving network of plasma associations.

A revolutionary concept, known as the Integrated Magnetic Optical Trap (IMOT), is poised to transform the field of trap physics. By fusing the principles of planar inductors and the technique of Optical Molecular Physics (OMP), IMOT seamlessly merges the advantages of magnetic and optical traps. Consequently, IMOT offers an expansive range of design possibilities for creating diverse types of traps, thereby expanding the range of applications in physics and biology that can benefit from this technology. Furthermore, IMOT presents a significant opportunity for significant cost savings and enhanced functional capabilities, making it a highly accessible tool for a broad range of researchers and scientists.

The spherically-symmetric accretion of a kinetic model onto a Schwarzschild black hole from a sphere of finite radius is investigated. The model utilizes a Boltzmannian distribution with rotational momentum consideration, weighted by a Maxwell-Boltzmann factor due to the gravitational potential. Employing a series expansion in terms of rotational momentum and Poincaré transformation, the angular momentum distribution is calculated. Consequently, the mass accretion rate is derived using a spherical tensor formalism and a point-mass approximation for collisionless accretion. Two distinct methods for estimating the mass accretion rate are explored, resulting in an expression for adiabatic incompressible accretion and a supplementary correction for finite radial initial conditions. For the special case of hydrodynamic accretion (thermal equilibrium), the model simplifies to the classic Bondi accretion scenario.

We are investigating the electromagnetic radiation that is emitted from an atom that is positioned in front of a thin, perfectly conductive mirror when the atom is experiencing horizontal horizontal motion. The atom's energy is initially raised to an excited state and we are considering a scenario where its initial velocity is parallel to the mirror and we are interested in finding the total radiation emitted in the direction of the atom's initial motion. Our research shows that this total radiation amounts to several tens of percentages of the radiation that would be emitted if the atom were not moving, and we have developed a theoretical model to explain these findings. The emitted radiation is stimulated by the atom's motion and we are analyzing its spectrum as well as the relationships between the radiation's time-dependent characteristics, its intensity, and the atom's rapid relative velocity.

A recent photometric study of the young cluster Westerlund 2 has revealed 11 bright massive stars and 8 additional O-type stars, bringing the total count to 19. Among these, seven are new discoveries, with six located near the cluster's core and one located further out. The cluster's core, once thought to be entirely composed of O-type stars, is now seen to have a diverse population. However, further studies are needed to confirm the origins and spatial distribution of these stars.

In the field of document processing, it's often necessary to remove noise from damaged documents before they can be read, a task that's typically done manually with time-consuming and labor-intensive efforts. To automate this process, a versatile model that can enhance both text and images is required, posing challenges in developing an effective approach. To address this, we employ a multi-task adversarial network that's comprised of sub-networks responsible for text restoration, image restoration, feature extraction, and classification, all working together to extract noise from documents and distinguish it from clean text. Our model utilizes a self-encoding mechanism with shared features to extract noise characteristics, allowing it to distinguish between noise and clean text at the highest level. Notably, our model is capable of providing a probability score that indicates the likelihood of a character being noisy, serving as an alternative to traditional noise removal methods that solely focus on noise elimination. To further personalize the noise removal process, we create a customized loss function that adapts the model's performance to specific data distributions. We test our model on the SIIER13 dataset and compare its performance with other state-of-the-art methods, showcasing its superiority in terms of overall restoration results, noise reduction, and the reliability of the resulting cleaned text for actual document use.

The growth of Information Technology has significantly altered how information is shared, making it necessary to convert printed documents into digital formats.  There has been an increase in fraudulent activities lately.  To prevent such crimes, it is crucial to identify and process identification documents accurately.  This processing is usually done manually, but it is time-consuming and labor-intensive.  To streamline this task, a solution using ID card extractor based on Optical Character Recognition and Natural Language Analysis was implemented, aiming to automate the extraction of essential identification information.  Optical Character Recognition ensures that the text on the ID card can be read, while Natural Language Analysis is used to enhance the accuracy of the extraction results by correcting any errors.  To evaluate the system's effectiveness, statistical measures were employed to assess its accuracy.  The research resulted in a satisfactory outcome, and the findings were presented in this research.

In vehicular networks, the unpredictable nature of 802.11p wireless communication systems poses challenges for reliable and real-time data transmission. The increasing demand for in-vehicle intelligence necessitates efficient channel assessment to guarantee satisfactory network performance. This paper addresses the above issue by introducing a temporal averaging LSTM-based channel assessment scheme for 802.11p, aimed at enhancing the fairness of channel access for vehicle nodes. The proposed solution employs a long short-term memory (LSTM) network to forecast a vehicle's transmission priority at a specific frame, based on historical data. This forecast is combined with a temporal averaging method to determine the vehicle's priority for the current frame. The proposed scheme is evaluated through simulations and shown to effectively mitigate channel access unfairness.

The process of restoring and enriching astronomical images has long been a pressing concern in the field of cosmology, critical to understanding the universe's complex phenomena. Historically, image enhancement techniques relied on fixed, predetermined processes but the vast majority of these methods remain unsuitable for images of celestial bodies, particularly as they often introduce noise and distort the original data. More importantly, the goal of image restoration is not solely to retrieve an original image but also to create a hypothetical, undistorted version of the observed scene, which is a task that requires significant creative expertise. In recent years, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been successfully applied to various CE tasks, producing high-quality results, which has prompted us to adopt a similar approach for colorizing and enhancing astronomical images. In this research, we propose the use of PCANet, a GAN-based method that incorporates Principal Component Analysis, to create colorful and vivid Celestial Body Imagery. The efficacy of PCANet is demonstrated through an analysis of the results on multiple astronomical datasets, which shows the superiority of the model over a comparison GAN-based method, specifically when evaluated using CE metrics such as PSNR and SSIM. Furthermore, we provide a series of visual comparisons that illustrate the ability of PCANet to produce high-quality colorized and enhanced astronomical images, which is further supported by expert feedback.

We've developed a novel neural network architecture called SUnN, differing from traditional multilayer perceptrons in its dependency on the input vector's norm. The output is represented as a difference in projections onto distinct convex polytopes. The norm of the input is utilized to segment the network into separate trainable components, effectively decoupling them. Consequently, this design exempts the neural network from the limitations of the backpropagation learning algorithm. Furthermore, we've proven that even with randomly initialized weights, the norm of the input is sufficient to achieve approximately equal classification outcomes across distinct classes. Consequently, this design facilitates the integration of deep neural networks with unsupervised regression predictive pre-training without necessitating significant resource-intensive parameter adjustments.

The ECFA Early Career Researcher's (ECR) committee aims to promote and engage in activities that benefit young research teams and individual ECRs across the full range of research domains covered by ECFA, including accelerator physics, beam physics, detector research, and associated software and computing. Formed in 2020 to address the unique challenges posed by the COVID-19 pandemic, the committee has successfully organized various events and initiatives to support the well-being of ECRs and foster a sense of community within the ECFA community. In its second term, the committee continued to prioritize aiding ECRs in navigating the consequences of the pandemic and explored ways to leverage digital tools to enhance collaboration and communication. In this report, the committee's structure, accomplishments, and the range of activities it initiated or supported are detailed, along with an overview of its plans for the upcoming years.

Recent breakthroughs in controlling light, made possible by advances in metamaterials, have led to significant interests in developing new optical devices. Researchers have now designed a new type of dual metasurface that can manipulate both optical and radio waves. This dual metasurface has unique properties, allowing it to reflect and steer optical ripples, as well as direct and control radio waves. The team successfully demonstrates optical ripples steering using this metasurface, presenting a new approach for optical applications.

This paper addresses the challenge of designing cognitive architectures for large-scale collaborative human-robot learning applications, involving hundreds of humans and robots. We present a scalable and open architecture for integrating multiple AI technologies to develop adaptive collaborative agents through artificial intelligence learning. The proposed architecture is flexible in its structure and agent composition, enabling it to be applied in various real-world scenarios, as demonstrated by our integration of existing AI technologies to create adaptive agents in two such scenarios. The architecture's key features include (1) a unified collaborative agent model; (2) a scalable multi-agent platform for large-scale experiments; and (3) adjustable parameters for guiding AI-driven agent adaptation. Our integration of AI technologies in two scenarios involves using organ donor registration system data to create an AI model for predicting organ donation eligibility and a healthcare-related online negotiation agent based on reinforcement learning. The latter agent's source code has been openly shared on GitHub, while details of the former's model are available on GitHub as well.

The mean absolute deviation is commonly assessed as a measure of variation within a set of data. When attempting to estimate this measure on a smaller subset of data, a conventional approach involves making adjustments to account for bias. These adjustments aim to compensate for the underestimation that typically occurs when using the sample median's mean absolute deviation as an estimate. In our research, we provide an alternative, corrected estimator that also addresses bias in the estimator's limits of convergence. Although the new estimator features the same convergence properties as the standard approach, its limits of convergence are more accurate, bringing it closer to the theoretical mean absolute deviation.

The accuracy of relation extraction can be increased by utilizing knowledge graph link prediction, according to our proposed strategy. To achieve this, we're incorporating knowledge graph embeddings into neural network-based models for relation extraction. These knowledge graph embeddings are, in turn, trained using the predictions made by the model for relation extraction. This mutually informative training process allows the two systems to effectively learn and adapt together. We've tested this approach with various knowledge graph embeddings and relation extraction models, including those that utilize attention and bidirectional grammer-based context-free parsing. Our findings indicate that this methodology yields significant improvements in relation extraction accuracy, with increases ranging from 1.4% to 4.6% absolute for the datasets we tested.

The behavior of anisotropic momentum in a quasi-particle N-dimensional N-dimensional QCD-like system is examined, taking into account the properties of anisotropic thermal medium and its influence on the quarkonium state. The characteristics of anisotropic momentum, such as its dissociation characteristics, binding energy, and root-mean-square distance between quark and antiquark, are studied in the quasi-particle Debye mass model with finite baryonic chemical potential. The results obtained are compared with those of the zero chemical potential case and the potential model calculations.

Our study focused on the magnetic arrangements within the crystals of Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7 using neutron-diffraction experiments. In Tb3RuO7, neighboring ruthenium atoms created a chain pattern, with some being ordered magnetically and others remaining randomly aligned. This unique combination resulted in an intermediate disordered state, with the ruthenium atoms exhibiting both ordered and uncertain magnetic arrangements within the crystals. In Nd3RuO7, the magnetic patterns followed the rules of symmetry, with all ruthenium atoms evenly ordered in a straight line. Differences between these two crystals, with Tb3RuO7 exhibiting disordered states and Nd3RuO7 in an ordered state, led us to conclude that the presence of disordered states within Tb3RuO7 was a result of the magnetic arrangements, rather than the crystal structure, solely controlling the disorder.

Our approach introduces modulated periodic activations, enabling the generated
images to better reflect the input data by utilizing the signal's frequency
content. In contrast to existing image synthesis methods that primarily focus on
aggregating pixel information, our algorithm effectively combines spatial and
temporal characteristics to produce high-resolution visual representations of
the input. Additionally, our method employs modulated periodic activations to
produce detailed functional illustrations of complex data entities, such as
images and text, resulting in beneficial latent dynamics for manipulation and
generalization purposes. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated
visually and is supported by quantitative evaluation on various benchmark
datasets. Moreover, the generated images and functional illustrations exhibit
exceptional realism and are capable of the level of detail required for
practical applications in the field.

We propose a novel approach to covariate-shift adaptation in supervised learning by utilizing a semi-supervised model that separates its causal and effective features. This 'Semi-Generative Model' employs two components: a probability model for causal features and a conditional model for effective features given the causal ones. By doing so, it accounts for distribution shifts in the data by isolating causes and effects and enabling the incorporation of unseen causes and effects in adapted learning. Our comprehensive framework encompasses three fundamental research questions: whether semi-generative models are effective, whether they can be learned from data, and whether they can be estimated from posterior distributions. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this model in coping with distribution shifts and highlight its potential to enhance supervised learning when the relationships between causes and effects are unclear or highly complex.

Despite its impressive task execution capabilities, the inner workings of deep learning systems remain shrouded in theoretical uncertainty. In our study, we establish a geometric model of deep learning by incorporating previously established discrete models, which we refine to obtain meaningful geometric and topological interpretations. Our novel model facilitates the exploration of neural network geometry and enables the visualization of neural network configurations through geometric and topological transformations. Furthermore, this framework allows us to investigate the continuity of learned parameters and to distinguish between meaningful and meaningless transformations, which we employ to assess the effectiveness of different training methods.

Elkington and Marsh have recently introduced a concept that relates to local minima within a lattice structure, where a local minimum is defined as a point where all neighboring points have a higher energy value. In this work, we explore this concept further by examining its significance in machine learning, where it may be referred to as 'local optima'. Our analysis focuses on the map of optima, which can be thought of as a digraph where nodes represent local optima and directed lines connect points that are in relation to each other. Our results show that this map has an inherent property where the distance between any two nodes is bounded by a certain constant multiplied by the dimensionality of the space. This finding is comparable to a similar theorem proposed by Conjecture, where it was assumed that local minima on a sphere would demonstrate similar properties. Our results, however, do not rely on the spherical model but rather follow from the machine learning principles of the layout of local optima. Where the map of optima may exhibit dense properties with regards to the coverage of the state space, particularly in scenarios where the function in question is random in nature. This has led to the notion of a critical threshold, denoted as c, where the map of optima becomes densely connected if the function has a constant value distribution on the lattice. If such a function does not adhere to this distribution, particularly in cases where it may have multiple valued properties, then the map of optima may not necessarily be densely

In jet substructure analysis, jet clustering methods are used to understand sub-jets within larger jets, enabling the identification of complex objects such as boosted hadronically decaying bosons and dark matter signatures. However, interpreting the decisions of these tools is challenging due to their complex structure. To gain insight into their functioning, researchers examined the individual contributions of expert variables, derived from the properties of the parent jet, to its assignment to a particular jet cluster. By propagating relevance backwards from the final classification layer to the input level, researchers identified the essential variables used by the algorithm to make that assignment. Furthermore, researchers modified the standard training procedure to include this layerwise relevance and found that this led to an increase in the accuracy and robustness of the algorithm.

For every positive integer k, a specific kind of Stirling number is defined as r-St(k,n), which represents the number of ways to divide a set of k items into n subsets. This paper presents specific formulas for the differences between consecutive terms of r-St(k,n) and the differences between consecutive terms of r-cat(n,k), which is another defined set. To simplify these formulas, the paper uses a specific relationship between two types of hypergeometric functions. This result can be compared to a similar formula for the differences between consecutive terms of the ordinary Stirling numbers.

The data presented in this table complements the work by A. L. Stamps et al. in their review "Multiferroic materials," published in 2015, by listing the possible irreducible representations for atoms located within interatomic double layers in those materials. The table includes information about 32 crystal symmetries, using the ten Datasheet 1 configurations to simplify the identification of relevant representations based on site symmetry. By referencing the tables, the potential ground states and symmetries of specific multiferroic materials, such as double ferrielectric and non-compact piezoelectric materials, can be quickly determined.

Momentum operators with geometric significance have been extensively explored in general relativity. This momentum is tied to Killing vectors, which have distinct properties as either tangential to geodesics or altering distances along geodesic curves. We're specifically interested in Killing vectors whose associated momentum is linked to integral curves, an aspect we investigate in this study. Our analysis demonstrates that such momentum operators are not sufficient for representing the spacetime transformation, indicating a lack of observability in terms of spacetime geometry. This analysis also discusses the implications of our findings within the context of the de Sitter spacetime.

The Hubbard model is a fundamental model for studying electronic interactions in condensed matter physics, often used to investigate the signs and patterns of quantum wavefunctions. However, the sign problem in quantum Monte Carlo simulations can be devastating, limiting the region of integrable parameters and making the solution difficult to achieve. Researchers have now explored the use of a complex-valued feedforward neural network to approximate the ground state of the Hubbard model, a strategy that has been successful in similar contexts and has the potential to be extended to more complex systems. The results show that this approach is efficient, reliable, and doesn't depend on a specific U/V ratio for starting the ground state, the integration parameters in the quantum Monte Carlo method. The ground states obtained have the correct signs for a 4-site ring system, and the strategy is expected to be adaptable to larger systems and more intricate models.

In composite Higgs theories, where the flavor symmetries are $G_F$ and the associated gauge symmetries are $G$, our analysis considers the case where the flavor and gauge symmetries have a common group structure, allowing us to simplify the flavor and the  composite  Higgs  models.  Specifically,  the  flavor  model  can  be  modeled  as  an  $G_F$ / $\mathbb{Z}_2$ principal bundle and the  Higgs model as an $G$ / $\mathbb{Z}_2$ principal bundle. Our work generalizes previous research in Flavon-Higgs theories by removing restrictions on the flavor and gauge groups. Our results include the determination of the flavored Higgs condensate and flavored flavor symmetry breaking in relation to the flavored Flavon-Higgs coset space. Our analysis also addresses the behavior of gauge boson mass spectra and flavor-diagonal scalar potential, while exploring the flavor and gauge symmetries in the flavored Flavon-Higgs theory. Our findings demonstrate that this theory is analogous to its flavor-symmetric counterpart, yet differs in flavor non-symmetric elements. Our work delves into the flavored Flavon-Higgs theory an essential component of composite Higgs models, where the flavor and gauge groups exhibit a significant correlation. Our analysis has broader implications in understanding the flavored Flavon-Higgs theory in relation to the flavor and gauge groups. Our results have further

The shift in the VR industry towards user-centered and immersive experiences will continue to gain momentum in the near future, driven by advancements in technology and the growing demand for engaging scenarios. To take advantage of the opportunities in this space, researchers and developers must gain insight into people's perceptions and behaviors within VR environments, which often differs from the classical perception theory. This paper highlights the need to understand the unknown aspects of user perceptions in VR and suggests a framework for identifying and addressing the challenges associated with perceptual distortions in VR application development.

To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we integrate German and Korean into BigScience's big-benchmark model, originally consisting of 49 languages, and analyze its performance with adapted and unmodified models. Our study investigates BigScience's Portuguese subset and compares models' results using both adapted and fixed vocabulary. Notably, the successful integration of German and Korean brings the total number of languages in BigScience's benchmark to 52.

Recent high-resolution observations using VLA and CARMA telescopes have unveiled previously unknown details of the binary system NR 6333 Aab. The derived properties for the two stars, such as their masses, radii, and luminosities, have been accurately determined through a careful analysis of observations and theoretical modeling. The findings indicate that both stars have masses approximately 1.17 and 1.13 times that of our Sun. The data also suggest the presence of the classic Miller & Maloney effect, a phenomenon where the mass ratio of the two stars differs from the expected value of 1, due to interactions and mass transfer between the binaries. The study further includes a theoretical modeling of binary system formation using a computational tool, for a specific scenario to see how the mass distribution of the system changes as it develops from a rotating core. The findings from this computational model are compared with the data from NR 6333 Aab to see how the system may have evolved.

This research introduces the m-ar-K-fast AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average with External Components (mar-K-FARIMC) model, an enhanced version of the classic FARIMC analysis, which is a combination of ARIMA and IMA components. The mar-K-FARIMC model is an innovation in the field of time series component analysis and is capable of identifying linear and nonlinear relationships, as well as ignoring insignificant variables. Our study validates the effectiveness of the mar-FARIMC algorithm by employing various datasets and challenge problems, which demonstrates its superiority over traditional methods. Additionally, we discuss the feasibility of developing the mar-FARIMC model into a machine learning-based hybrid approach to facilitate its practical application in real-world problems.

This paper builds on existing research linking finite model theory to algebraic and propositional proof systems. It's proven that if a logic system can identify unique, non-isomorphic graphs in a specific category, then a related proof system can do so as well, at roughly the same computational cost. This allows researchers to apply existing bounds from the latter system to the former, shedding new light on CPT's limitations. Establishing a polynomial CPT lower bound via a related PTIME-instance could resolve a long-standing question in finite model theory. Additionally, the findings provide a theoretical explanation for the separation between polynomial calculus and extended polynomial calculus within bounded-degree settings.

A full transformation ring $T_n$ is defined as the set of all linear transformations on an $n$-dimensional vector space that have a finite order in terms of matrix representation. We prove in this paper that the ring $R_n$ of germs of full transformation rings $T_n$ under the partial order of finiteness is a sigma-rings under the given conditions. This provides a new endless family of sigma-rings in addition to the known examples.

When evaluating claims that are untestable, the assessment process faces a significant challenge. To address this issue, we develop a framework that enables objective comparison of comparable claims. Through the application of lexicographic ordering, the theoretical model incorporates (1) the approximate likelihood of each claim as assessed subjectively and (2) the claims' ranks in terms of their perceived benefits. Additionally, the framework considers (3) the claims' ranks in terms of their adverse consequences and (4) the claims' ranks in terms of their alignment with prior knowledge. We demonstrate the efficacy of our framework in a practical scenario, where it facilitates the identification of the most promising claims across various areas of research in healthcare, even in cases where direct evidence is scarce.

Incident detection on social media has garnered significant interest due to the vast potential of social media data to supply context-free and context-based information. However, the current methods for identifying incidents on social media are plagued by significant difficulties, including the inability to verify the accuracy of available data and the need to distinguish high-quality posts from low-quality ones. To address these limitations, this paper employs a robust stream-processing technique for detecting incidents on social media in real-time. To filter out irrelevant information and pinpoint incidents, it utilizes a data flow-based approach featuring a combination of geospatial, temporal, and contextual filtering. To identify unusual behavior, it also utilizes the One-Class SVM algorithm supported by social media data. To assess the accuracy of the posts, it employs a data-driven method that takes into account the social media network's structural characteristics, as well as the statistical measures of posts, including frequency and density. To evaluate the efficacy of our approach, this paper demonstrates real-time incident detection on social media in two case studies and compares it with existing methods that rely on location data.

New, high-precision data from the cosmic microwave background lensing measurements and tomographic galaxy surveys in the upcoming years will enable more efficient cross-correlation analysis. We examine the usefulness of the weighted skew-spectrum as an optimal estimator of angular bispectrum amplitude in extracting non-Gaussian information on both galaxy bias and cosmological parameters, achieved through deep bispectrum-decomposition-based bias modeling without computational scalar field limitations. We apply this method to the skewing of CMB lensing and temperature data versus galaxy surveys, focusing on the potential gains from using higher-order analysis than the skew-spectrum. We found that the bispectrum-based skew-spectrum provides the strongest signal-to-noise ratio in the large-scale structure large-scale structure, when compared to the conventional skew-spectrum from the galaxy power spectrum. Interestingly, we found that the CMB lensing and temperature data provide the best signal-to-noise ratio when analyzed up to the fourth skew-spectrum order, largely due to the quasi-projection of CMB lensing on the largest scales and the relatively clean non-Gaussian component extraction. Moreover, we found that the CMB lensing and temperature data provide the best constraints on the neutrino mass, with a 20-sigma precision, when analyzed up to the fourth skew-spectrum order, largely due to the quasi-projection of CMB lensing on the largest scales and the relatively clean non-Gaussian component extraction.
