Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are emerging due to rising demands for accurate predictions and thorough analyses. However, they necessitate a considerable amount of computational power and time for processing. Previous studies on pruning have focused on enhancing inference efficiency, but there's also a need to improve training efficiency while accounting for the effects of pruning on model accuracy. Our proposed framework, ClickTrain, effectively and precisely balances the impact of pruning on both training speed and model precision, enabling the use of efficient models for accurate learning. By incorporating a novel pruning strategy and an efficient re-initialization technique, ClickTrain allows the model to accurately learn from its reinitialized weights, thereby enhancing overall training efficiency. Our experimental results confirm that ClickTrain surpasses current pruning-based training methods in both overall accuracy and convergence speed.

This research examines the addition of modal operators to the Distributive Complete Lambek Calculus (DCL), specifically their impact on soundness and the presence of non-deterministic proofs. DCL is an infinitary substructural logic with a specific sequent calculus framework, and it incorporates left and right division rules. By incorporating \box and \diamondsuit operators to the DCL sequent calculus, this paper presents soundness criteria for the resulting logic system. Furthermore, it characterizes the relationship between the \box\diamondsuit^n and \box^n\diamondsuit operators for any positive integer n, and proves the decidability of the resulting logic system.

The detections made by the Advanced LIGO and the Virgo for the third observing period have brought us significantly closer to understanding how the collisions of compact objects emit gravitational waves. Researchers now have the capability to make detailed analyses of the gravitational waves emitted from these events, understanding their characteristics in great depth, which has led to a need for more sophisticated methods to categorize the collisions based on their properties. A recent breakthrough innovation has the potential to take collision identification and classification to an unprecedented level of precision and depth of information, using the fundamental properties of the gravitational waves themselves to make the classification. We present a new deep learning approach to making the classification, which utilizes a combination of fundamental properties of the gravitational waves and how they are spread out in space and time, as well as the simulation-based signal characteristics, which includes the impact of external matter on the gravitational waves. Our results show that a well-designed neural network has the capability to make the classification with remarkable precision, using the fundamental properties of the gravitational waves and their simulation-based characteristics. Which has significant potential to take collision identification and classification to new heights?

A new discovery has been made regarding a gas giant exoplanet, which orbits around a star called TOI-5542 approximately every 7.2 days. This exoplanet, which we refer to as TOI-5542b, has been verified through a combination of data from the TESS satellite and hand-crafted images taken with the SOAR adaptive optics camera. This verification has confirmed that TOI-5542b has a minimum mass of about 1.13 Jupiter masses and a radius of approximately 1.23 times that of Jupiter. Initial estimates suggest that TOI-5542b is about 8 billion years old. Additionally, a detailed age estimate based on a model that takes into account the activity level of TOI-5542 has determined that this exoplanet is likely older than 8 billion years. This makes TOI-5542b one of the oldest warm Jupiter planets discovered so far. Further analysis of the star and exoplanet properties has revealed certain distinct qualities, which could provide valuable insights into the formation and evolution of this particular planetary system.

Optimal decision-making under uncertainty with limited resources can be guided by the Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP). Like in the classical Markov Decision Process, the goals in the CMDP are to maximize rewards and minimize costs, but with the added constraint of limited resources. Theoretical foundations of CMDP exist, but finding the optimal policy proves to be computationally expensive. This study proposes a primal-dual algorithm named Primal-Dual Optimistic Lower Bound (PDOB) that provides a constant factor approximation with a linear computational expense. Theoretical analysis shows that the efficiency of PDOB is the best achievable given existing constraints. Moreover, experiments with various scenarios confirm that PDOB achieves high quality policies.

Many educational resources, particularly those that are printed or digital, struggle with accessibility due to visual impairments or connectivity issues. Recent advancements in Artificial Intelligence and Deep Learning have significantly improved the recognition accuracy of handwritten characters, but mathematical notation specific challenges still persist. This project addresses these challenges by developing an end-to-end system for recognizing offline handwritten mathematical expressions in a structured format. This involves using a custom, derived dataset from the MathAI Challenge and integrating a Symbol Prior Network to enhance the recognition of complex mathematical expressions. Comprehensive evaluations were conducted using evaluation metrics specifically designed for mathematical expression analysis. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, with a recall of 44.53% and a precision of 43.76% within a recall range of 20% to 100%. This high performance is attributed to the combination of a robust sequence-to-sequence model and the Symbol Prior Network, which addresses the inherent challenges of recognizing offline handwritten mathematical expressions.

We examine a set of supersymmetric quantum field theories with a high level of supersymmetry in various dimensions. By utilizing mathematical concepts from the study of algebraic geometry, particularly the development of the cohomology of sheaves, we explore how these theories interact with the structure of their underlying geometric frameworks. Case studies involves models of supersymmetric quantum field theories in both two and three-dimensional environments, and we find that the general principles of geometric coherence apply universally, independent of the level of supersymmetry. However, the intricate relationships between quantum field theories and their geometric frameworks become particularly complex in cases with a lack of free fermion charges, leading to novel and hard-to-predict outcomes in such scenarios.

When analyzing complex networks, a fractionated network model is employed to study their inherent characteristics and link dynamics. This involves dividing the network into separate components and observing their interplay. Our research involves segmenting a complex network into two subsystems, studying their individual behavior and interactions, and examining how their connection impacts the overall system dynamics upon reassembling the fractions. We discover that the network's fundamental characteristics are influenced by the variability of the interaction process and the differences in behavior between the separated subsystems. Additionally, our findings indicate that a high level of interaction instability among components exacerbates the discrepancies in their behavior, while a more even distribution of interactions within the subsystems minimizes these differences and, in turn, the variability of the system dynamics upon reassembling the fractions.

Actor-critic reinforcement learning has significant practical applications and has been extensively explored, with adaptations in various forms to tackle different challenges. One common variant is the post-critique method, which combines policy gradient with value function estimation through critic networks. Notably, this post-critique form of actor-critic reinforcement learning yields more efficient exploration of new states. Despite its advantages, it sometimes results in the actor network learning unnecessary details that can increase noise during exploration, ultimately hindering its performance. In contrast, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) method is known for its efficient exploration of non-linear parameter spaces; however, its primary use is for sampling. In this research, a novel approach called Hamiltonian Policy Gradient (HPG) is proposed, which submers the actor network with an HMC sampler at intervals to optimize its exploration. Moreover, a double post-critique variant called HPCG has also been created by integrating the benefits of both techniques. Experimental outcomes show that these new methods outperform a traditional post-critique actor-critic network as well as an HMC-based sampling method when used in reinforcement learning settings.

It's widely accepted that there are infinitely many twin primes, with most mathematicians relying on the conjecture that $P(x)$, a specific polynomial related to prime numbers, is negative for positive $x$ values. This paper provides a straightforward proof of the twin prime conjecture by first demonstrating that $P(x)$ being negative for all $x > 2$ implies the prime number theorem (PTC), with the PTC then confirming the existence of infinitely many twin primes.

Autonomous vehicles in enclosed spaces face challenges such as collisions and navigation path disruptions due to limited range sonar sensors. To address this, researchers proposed an enhanced navigation system for indoor vehicle guidance. This study outlines a sonar fusion strategy to mitigate these issues and improve upon existing single-sensor approaches. The proposed method incorporates an adaptive sonar fusion algorithm to merge data from multiple sonar sensors, resulting in a more complete and accurate picture of the environment. Furthermore, a dynamic obstacle detection system has been developed to identify obstacles within the sonar's limited range and flag them for the controller to adjust the vehicle's path. The effectiveness of this solution was demonstrated in simulations and real-world tests, showcasing its ability to accurately detect obstacles and contribute positively to the vehicle's navigation system.

Compositional analyses of NII Nereid's surface, the moon orbiting Neptune, provide the opportunity to explore the geological activity of outer solar system satellites. Nereid's near-infrared reflectance is examined to identify the presence of water ice and its mixtures with other minerals. Spectra from Nereid and Neptune's moon Halimede and Phoebe are compared to models of portlandite and ammonium chloride water ice mixtures. Nereid's spectrum between 0.8 and 2.4 micrometers is dominated by a red continuum thought to originate from primordial water ice. Spectral features around 1.5 micrometers are reproduced by combining ice models with a red slope, and Nereid's spectrum between 2.8 and 4.2 micrometers is characterized by a superimposed absorption band at 3.1 micrometers. We attribute the absorption to CH4 and water ice containing various ferroan minerals. Spectra from Nereid and Halimede are used to derive the absorption coefficient lambda~a0.72 mu m, and Nereid's spectrum is used to determine the absorption band strength. Our results for Nereid are compared to those of Halimede and Phoebe, and the implications for Nereid's composition and surface temperature are explored. We estimate the depth of the photosphere to be 0.4-1.5 meters, and the presence

Let $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$ be the ring of lower triangular matrices of order $n \geq 2$, consisting of elements from the finite field $F(q)$ of order $q \geq 2$. Additionally, let $V_{2n}(q)$ be the free left module of its counterpart $\mathcal{M}_n(q)$. This study reveals that over the ring $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$, especially when $n$ is even and $q$ is odd, the dual space $V_{2n}(q)$ exhibits the properties of an affine plane, while when $n$ is even or odd and $q$ is an even number, $V_{2n}(q)$ turns out to be a projective plane. Importantly, it is also established that over the even-order ring $\mathcal{R}_{2n}(q)$, especially when $n$ is greater than or equal to $2$ and $q$ is odd, the free right module $V_{2n}(q)$ acts as a projective plane.

This study introduces a means of comparing Ramsey-like statements by utilizing models, thereby establishing a continuum hypothesis ($CH$) that sits at the center of a hierarchy of statements ranked under the Tukey-like preorder established by Pawlikowski. We also explore relationships between these statements and $CH$ within the context of continuous real functions.

A new resource-efficient method for improving policy outcomes is introduced, which fine-tunes a policy's operation in accordance with the principles of a known causal model derived from observational data, with the objective of enhancing the policy's performance as measured by a metric called negativity in the causal model. The idea behind this method is that a an optimal policy existing in the space of possible interventions can be targeted, which has the property of minimizing the causal model's negativity and is closest to a set of policies consistent with the observed data. The Bayesian learning framework is used to determine the optimal target for the policy, which is a posterior mode in the space of possible interventions, which has been shown to be a consistent estimator for the optimal target. A sequence of randomized policies is constructed by iteratively refining the target, which has been proven to converge asymptotically to the optimal target, which has the property of being the closest point in the space of possible interventions to the posterior mode. The convergence rate is known to be geometric and the results are known to be robust to a variety of common assumptions concerning the structure of the causal model and the availability of data, which are based on the characteristics of the Polya gamma distribution. The method is known to be computationally efficient and is known to be capable of adapting to a variety of different amounts of data, which is based on the method's application of a Laplace approximation for computing the posterior distribution. The method is known to be a variant of the sample splitting approach

Dualities, a concept of category theory, describe duality relationships between categories. Research has focused on determining the specific categories that satisfy certain dualities when given certain conditions. This study establishes new categories that fit certain dualities called "ring theory duality" and "module testing dualities," which are tested for their relationships with established theories such as dimension theory, the Dowling-Wagner formula, and the Krull-Siegel theorem.

A proposed $E_8$ network system is presented as a method to tackle the host-guest physics of a specific type of material, with the guest species being the bosonic phonons within the host material. The $E_8$ group's properties are utilized to develop a strategy for identifying suitable configurations that exhibit quantized interactions with the phonons as the material's chemical potential is varied. This approach results in a range of potential phase transition states, along with other unusual phase transition types, such as scenarios where the material's resistance suddenly increases. Furthermore, calculations of quantum entanglement and nontrivial contextuality for the core system using a specific $E_8$ rotation reveal significant amounts of both effects, which in scenarios like the double well potential point towards a quantum origin of entanglement and which in scenarios like the three-well potential indicate entanglement's contribution.

A model has been created that generates mock Landau levels using smooth, non-discrete bands with zero curvature, based on a special type of nontrivial band geometry. When interacting with an electron-like system, this mock band curvature acts as an effective attraction that could lead to superconductivity. Utilizing a modified version of Eliashberg's equations and a specialized approach to integrate out high-energy degrees of freedom, it is found that the system exhibits a wide range of superconducting properties that are influenced by the band geometry and a critical interaction strength. The results suggest that strong nontrivial band geometry can facilitate superconductivity even in the absence of it in the free system, and that the system's superconducting properties can be controlled through the band geometry.

The Gaussian distribution is uniquely determined by the distribution of a linear combination and a power function of independent identically distributed random variables. We identify the distributions of random variables in a 1-dimensional locally compact Abelian group, establishing a theorem analogous to the original Polya's theorem.

In the analysis of high-dimensional presence-absence data, the objective is to group samples based on their similarities in non-zero feature values. This is particularly relevant in fields like genomics, where the goal is to identify coherent groups of genes associated with specific phenotypes. The challenge lies in dealing with a large number of features that far exceed the number of observations, making traditional clustering methods ineffective. In response, researchers have developed and proposed a range of clustering methods tailored to high-dimensional data. In this paper, we provide an in-depth review of these techniques, followed by a comprehensive simulation study that compares their performance using synthetic data. The results of this study serve as a foundation for a subsequent case study, where we utilize these methods to analyze the GSE1736 microarray dataset, examining the empirical benefits of pre-processing the data in the presence of outliers.

In recent years, salient object detection using deep neural networks has received significant attention, but dealing with RGB and RGB-D images separately often necessitates the design of specific network architectures. This paper proposes an efficient and unified framework that integrates cross-attention context extraction to effectively tackle both tasks. By effectively fusing two inputs in the context extraction module, our framework leverages the rich information present in RGB-D images, thereby enhancing salient object detection. Furthermore, the proposed approach streamlines the process by eliminating the need for edge maps and auxiliary losses, thus facilitating easy extension to unsupervised settings. Experimental results demonstrate the framework's superiority over other state-of-the-art methods in terms of both performance and computational efficiency.

The UM-IU@LING system for Aggressive Detection in Spanish and English on SemEval 2019 Task 6 is presented. Our approach to aggressive tweet identification employed BERT for feature extraction, combining the outputs from BERT and SVM classifiers to determine the final features. SVMs were trained on the provided data sets for Spanish and English, with the goal of achieving optimal performance in micro-F1 score. To streamline the training process, a pre-trained BERT model was used, which was fine-tuned with the relevant data. Our best results consisted of a macro-F1 score of 0.7446 for Spanish and 0.8149 for English, both in the official evaluation settings.

A number, N, that can be expressed as a quotient of two palindromic numbers, P1 and P2, is called a palindromic quotient. In this paper, we explore the relationship between numbers that are quotients of palindromes and those that are not. It is demonstrated that both the set of palindromic quotients and its complement are infinite. Additionally, the paper establishes a finding that the set of palindromic quotients is dense within the set of all natural numbers greater than 1.

We present a novel approach to reconstructing images from polyenergetic computed tomography (CT) scans through a variational framework that involves a non-convex cost function. This four-dimensional cost function simultaneously optimizes and takes into account the varying energies, non-uniform noise, and multiple materials present in a scan. To overcome the hurdles posed by a non-convex objective function, we employ the alternating direction method of multi-parameters (ADMM) to break it down into smaller, more manageable components and iterate through them until an optimal solution is found. The effectiveness of this method is confirmed by our simulation-based experiments, which demonstrate that it yields reconstructions comparable to those produced by iterative algorithms tailored to specific tasks, while also showcasing its sensitivity to parameter selection.

This research introduces a novel approach in the field of Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR), focusing on the data generation stage, to produce diverse language writing systems from a single source. Typically, language models are trained using extensive datasets, but this is challenging for languages with limited resources. Our method overcomes this limitation by leveraging a reference transcript to create multiple artificial handwritings, enhancing the dataset with much-needed diversity. To evaluate its effectiveness, our technique was applied to a synthetic dataset of contrasting languages, showing positive results in a study utilizing the HTR pipeline with WaveNet and language models based on n-grams and unsupervised learning.

To merge results from different calculational methods for atomic nuclei,
particularly for heavy nuclei, it's crucial to merge calculations that were
conducting with and without employing relativistic effects. This is essential for
obtaining an integrated picture of the nuclear structure at both low and high
energies. However, merging calculations that were conducted with and without
relativistic effects is quite complicated due to the significant differences in
the resulting energy spectra. This paper discusses the procedure of merging
results from the relativistic and non-relativistic mean-field calculations for
heavy nuclei, specifically for nuclei comprising protons and neutrons from 40
through 120 and 1 through 30, respectively. The method entails comparing and
matching corresponding states, while accounting for potential ambiguities in the
mashing process. An analysis of the merged calculations in comparison to
experimental data on nuclear binding energy and mass is also presented. This
new approach of merging calculations facilitates thorough examinations of the
relativistic mean-field model, particularly its parameter dependence, and offers
a means to assess the significance of relativistic effects in nuclear binding.

We invite undergraduate students and early graduate students to an educational introduction to topological quantum phenomena, utilizing the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model as a conceptual framework. Through this model, we'll delve into various strategies for determining a quantum system's topological characteristics, such as its electron configuration, boundary behavior, and periodicity in momentum, as well as its correlation with the system's band structure. Additionally, we'll investigate the relationship between topological properties and the Hamiltonian's symmetry, leading to the emergence of key concepts in modern quantum physics, including Anderson localization, topological insulators and superconductors, and topological bands and invariants. The SSH model serves as an accessible and intuitive starting point for exploring these ideas within a quantum system that is both manageable and visualizable.

This study examines the compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces associated with certain bounded, convex domains in complex n-dimensional space containing non-trivial analytic circles in the boundary. Consequently, this characterizes compactness of the composition operator with a continuous symbol (limited to the unit disk) on the Bergman space of the polydisk.

We have derived a two-loop amplitude for four gravitons in AdS$_5$ times S$^5$ using a direct computational approach from the QFT perspective with an emphasis on symmetry properties. The amplitude was found by applying the Weyl transformation to a QFT correlation function, where the QFT correlation function was calculated via a Gaussian process. The QFT used in the correlation function involves nonlinear symmetries, specifically NAD/SPIN$(2N)$, where N equals 4, with an additional set of fermionic symmetries introduced to ensure the amplitude is graviton-specific. The QFT used has been well-documented as having a unique property where it is not associated with any potential changes in the gravity amplitude due to couplings with other fields, ensuring the amplitude remains pure graviton. The amplitude obtained was found to match the results from the supergravity path integral with two-loop efficiency when using the de Wit-Manouchehri package for supergravity amplitude computation with an emphasis on Gaugino cancellations.

The memory allocation process on GPUs is a complex task. The direct mapping of host memory to device memory leads to excessively large memory consumption by, for instance, a mesh object, limiting the number of simultaneous objects on a GPU. This limitation hinders the development of software that utilizes parallel processing on GPUs, necessitating an advanced memory allocation framework that can efficiently manage memory on the device. To resolve these issues, we introduce DynaSOAr, an innovative memory allocation library that employs a balance of small blocks and arbitrary-size objects to minimize memory usage and parallelization complexities. To achieve this, DynaSOAr leverages device-side bitmasks to rapidly identify and allocate memory blocks for objects of various sizes, utilizing a hash table for efficient management of the memory blocks. To facilitate smooth interaction between host and device, DynaSOAr provides a convenient API that enables seamless allocation and release of memory on both the host and device. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that DynaSOAr outperforms current solutions, successfully supporting simulation of diverse objects across various applications, with the added benefit of an easily adaptable API allowing developers to implement custom object types and multiple object creation scenarios.

This article revisits Standard Model unitary gauge theories based on an $U(1)_X$ gauge group and inspired by $SO(10)$, incorporating the Type-I and Type-II $U(1)_X$ gauge theories from 2009 and 2010. To achieve matching fermion content with the Standard Model, the $SO(10)$ model incorporates two $SU(2)_R$ gauge groups. The articles by Cheng, Kelley, and Zhang and by Ding, Zhou, and Li are extensively reviewed, with their findings and methods reevaluated. Additionally, we examine the consistency of the Type-I and Type-II theories with the current dark matter and dark photon experimental data. We also compare our results with the ones previously obtained by Cheng, Kelley, and Zhang and by Ding, Zhou, and Li. This includes the dark matter mass and spin-dependent scattering cross-sections, as well as the dark photon mass and coupling to electron electric dipole moment. The dark matter relic density is calculated using both freeze-out and simulating the hot Big Bang scenario with the results of the $U(1)_X$ model. The analysis indicates that the dark matter mass is approximately 793 MeV, with a scattering cross-section of $10^{-41}\mathrm{GeV}^2$ and a dark photon mass of 137 MeV and coupling of $10^{-3}$ to the electromagnetic one. The electron electric dipole moment is found to be $10^{-20

A comprehensive study of a cane tube under pressure reveals its mechanical properties allow it to withstand crushing forces due to compressive yield in its wall. Through a combination of experimental measurement and theoretical modeling, analysts find that a cane tube subjected to internal pressure maintains its stability up to a certain point, after which any further increase in pressure causes the tube to elongate. To prevent the tube from collapsing radially, a specific level of pressure is needed; below this threshold, the tube is structurally stable in all directions. This research provides the foundation for a precise prediction of how much force a cane tube can withstand under different pressure conditions, ultimately enabling the design of more robust cane structures.

In various fields, ensuring decision-making confidence under uncertain conditions leads to a key concept known as epistemic robustness. This paper introduces a novel approach for quantifying the epistemic robustness of a belief state within a credal Bayesian network, which is carried out by comparing the belief's closure with the set of all possible belief states sharing the same first-order features. Due to the computational demands of this problem, we have adapted a different method that involves comparing cumulative distributions up to a specified order, effectively simplifying the inquiry into a higher-dimensional problem on probabilistic circuits. As a result, the epistemic robustness of a belief state can be obtained by inspecting its corresponding probabilistic circuit under a relaxed constraint, which enables an efficient approximation yielding a logarithmically scaled reduction in computational complexity compared to the original circuit's size. Moreover, this paper explores a corresponding query evaluation problem where the input set is a collection of credal Bayesian networks, which we resolve by adopting a different circuit representation known as Sum-of-Functions (SoF). Using the transformed SoF structure, we obtain a linear scaling in terms of circuit size and a constant dependency on the number of query variables, which significantly improves over existing approaches bearing complex dependencies and exponential or polynomial scalings.

The Wannier-Statz method, originally describing quantum tunneling in a periodic potential, has been effectively adopted to analyze acoustic wave behavior in ultrasonic applications. This approach has been successfully applied to study various phenomena such as acoustic Wannier-Statz states, their associated Buckling modes, and Wannier-Statz states with a non-integer index. Furthermore, this method has been used to investigate the Wannier-Statz structure of an ultrasonic device and predict Wannier-Statz states with unique properties that could be utilized for improved ultrasonic inspections.

In the realm of generalised quadrangles, we focus on transitive codes, a particular class of codes that exhibit an intriguing transitive property when their decoding centers are considered. This paper introduces two distinct types of transitive codes: those that maintain transitivity when neighbors are replaced and those with transitive automorphism groups. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the fourfold virutual spreads of the classical quadrangles form the sole non-trivial examples of codes that exhibit both properties. Partial spreads of classical quadrangles are also discussed; it is shown that every partial spread forms a neighbor-transitive code, and its automorphism group is either neighbor-transitive or has a specific intransitive structure.

The Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) in the Milky Way is an exceptional location to analyze star formation patterns and compare them with theoretical models due to its distinctive properties.  To understand the anisotropic structure of the CMZ more deeply, a two-dimensional correlation function is applied to a spatial density dataset obtained from 3D barionic gas data.  The results show a clear pattern of density fluctuations in a radial and elongated shape, significantly aligned with the CMZ's major axis.  The correlation function's breakdown into different components allows for the identification of three distinct groups, each representing a different level of density variation within the CMZ.  The findings from this study provide the most detailed information so far about the anisotropic properties of the CMZ's structure, offering insights into its physical and dynamical characteristics.

To accurately analyze changes in materials using X-ray Absorption Near Edge Spectroscopy (XANES), a mathematical framework is needed that can effectively simulate the absorption of high-fluence X-ray pulses and incorporate core-hole interactions. A proposed model, called the Electron Groups Model, is presented as an alternative to computational methods such as ab-initio and density functional theory. The model's electron groups are defined as independent entities that can move freely within specified regions, allowing for a physical interpretation of the model's outcomes. A fully-automated algorithm is also available to obtain the required mathematical coefficients for precise simulations. The model's efficacy is validated by comparing it with both first-principle calculations and experimental data for a case study involving nickel oxide.

This research develops a temperature sensor chip featuring an integrated temperature detector, analog-to-digital converter and correction circuitry. The temperature detector, which utilizes a sub-threshold CMOS op-amp-based circuit, offers precise temperature readings with minimal dynamic range for consumer electronics applications. The analog-to-digital converter leverages a two-stage fully-differential delta-sigma sampling method to ensure accuracy, while the correction circuitry facilitates effective internal temperature calibration. To optimize power efficiency, the detector and converter operate at varying frequencies, with the highest frequency during sampling and lower frequencies during holding modes. As a result, this design achieves a 0.6V - 1.8V operating voltage range, 0.24$^\circ$C resolution, $\pm$1.4$^\degree$C inaccuracy, 0.56$^\degree$C2 resolution, and features a power consumption of 2.95mW with a conversion period of 200ms, along with a 1.06nJ per conversion charge per degree integration. Moreover, the sensor's compact size of 80x80μm has made it suitable for use in industry-standard CMOS processes.

Quantum entanglement, a pivotal concept in quantum physics, holds the potential for revolutionizing various technologies such as quantum computing and communication. A common form of entanglement, bi-photon entanglement, is traditionally generated using parametric down-conversion and is used as a tool to study quantum phenomena and develop techniques for entanglement manipulation. However, the vast photon density gap between typical optical photons and polarized photons presents significant challenges for entanglement transfer and other applications. This issue can be overcome by employing the quantum scissors phenomenon to create polarized entanglement through a complex series of optical processes involving van der Waals interactions between carbon particles. Heralded generation of polarized entanglement using this method could provide a valuable source of entangled photons, as well as a unique system for studying the transfer of entanglement across distinct spectral domains.

This paper explores the concept of digital metric spaces and spanners within the context of these spaces. It starts by outlining the criteria for non-digital metric spaces to form geometric spanners, before investigating whether similar conditions apply in digital metric spaces to form digital geometric spanners. The authors introduce two new concepts: the unique digit spanner and the $\delta$-close unique digit spanner, and demonstrate their construction in digital Euclidean spaces. The research further examines the efficiency of these digital geometric spanners in terms of their stretch factor and number of nodes. The study specifically considers the effects of number of dimensions, number of points, and precision of the digital space on the spanners. The authors suggest that even in digital metric spaces, the conditions for forming geometric spanners are similar to their non-digital counterparts, and present evidence of this through the presented results, which also highlight the influence of digital space precision on geometric spanners.

Accurate IoT device identification is crucial, yet conventional methods are unacceptably expensive in terms of computational expense, memory usage, and monetary cost. To address these limitations, we suggest an efficient approach that effectively minimizes costs while achieving reliable results. To optimize the device identification process, we implement a costly cost-based feature extraction method in conjunction with a reliable classification technique. A restrictive measure is introduced to guarantee classification accuracy and subsequently reduce costs by identifying the most informative features. Thorough experimentation utilizing real-world data sets and multiple restraints has been conducted to confirm the high accuracy and significant cost reductions of our proposed method.

Godel modal logics can be associated with two types of structures: those formed by the relationship between worlds and their accessibility within a given set, and those formed by the relationship between worlds and their accessibility within a subset of worlds. Godel modal logics can also be linked to two types of algebraic systems: Blake systems and Montague systems. These systems are equivalent to the structures in terms of deductive power, with Montague systems being more powerful in extensions that include negation. Negation in Godel modal logics can be dually interpreted as either a universal or a particular negation, leading to two-layer nonclassical logics that are modal in nature. These logics can be represented using a granular algebra in the style of Dunn, with the addition of modal operators, and can also be associated with a special type of relational structure in which worlds have a universal and a particular negation aspect.

This research presents a novel and straightforward technique for word-alignment that leverages bilingual data from external sources like machine translation platforms. We demonstrate that a model with limited parameters can achieve performance comparable to GIZA++ when trained on just 2048 parameters and 12 epochs, using data sets like Euromillion and LDC2005-E18. Furthermore, this technique enables the automatic generation of word alignments for any language pair without requiring manual annotation.

We suggest an iterative method to find a Nash equilibrium in a general game with strategies represented by measurable functions. The algorithm's core is an operator Res, which transforms measurable functions into measurable operators, and the equivalence $x\geq x_{\operatorname{eq}}$ in a certain distance metric indicates that $x$ is closer to a Nash equilibrium than $x_{\operatorname{eq}}$. The algorithm's convergence is ensured by the Lusin-Rademacher theorem, and we provide a concrete example to illustrate the distortion concept.

This article serves as an introduction to the $m_\mathrm{PBDH}$ package, a specialized tool for predicting the characteristics of Primordial Black Hole Dark Matter (PBHDM) systems. Its functionality encompasses: 

 1. **Predicting PBHDM abundance**: The package utilizes the version 2.0 version of $\texttt{CosmoMC}$ to simulate the thermalization and decay of PBHs, along with their associated production rates. These simulations can be based on either the conventional adiabatic licelihood analysis or the more recent $f(Ri)$ model.
2. **Post-formation PBDH characteristics**: The package includes sub-routines to determine the physical properties of the PBHs, such as their mass and radial distance, following from the $f(Ri)$ model.
3. **Microphysical considerations**: The package incorporates equations relevant to the PBHs' physical properties, such as their radius and surface gravity, along with their maximum orbital distances around the Milky Way's baryonic matter.
4. **Graphical illustrations**: Various plots are provided in this article to demonstrate the tool's capabilities, which can be achieved through three distinct methods: (i) utilizing $\texttt{CosmoMC}$'s built-in plots; (ii) generating customized plots using $\texttt{matplotlib}$ and $\texttt{aste}"; (iii) incorporating $\texttt{healpy}$ to create 2D squared

We conducted molecular-dynamics simulations to study the uniform and non-uniform phases in a system consisting of rigid wedge-shaped molecules, with each wedge composed of four connected spheres that allow for free movement within a confined space. The study revealed that in addition to a hexagonal close-packed structure, there exists a tetragonal phase characterized by a 90-degree angle and a ratio of areas of 2:1, resulting from the modulation of wedge tips. Furthermore, this splay pattern led to the emergence of tetragonal and monoclinic phases with specific symmetry properties. The simulation results were supported by computer-generated images and an in-depth analysis of the entropic and interaction energies within the system.

This work investigates multivariate Gaussian fields (GFields) confined to the surface of a sphere, focusing on their spectral analysis. The study centers around developing straightforward, one-step recurrence relationships in Gaussian covariance matrices to facilitate the transformation of the spatial covariance structure in GFields. This allows for a range of applications, including the calculation of the maximal theoretical information gain and the determination of the best可approximating polynomial degree for a given field, along with assessing its representability through a trigonometric polynomial.

A long-standing obstacle in practical quantum communication has been overcome, namely, enabling a single person to visually perceive a quantum message without a detector being present. This challenge, framed as a single-pixel visualization problem, has been theoretically solved using the Mach-Zehnder interferometer and a quantum entanglement technique. Notably, this solution remains valid even in the presence of noisy systems and individual photon emission processes. To prove this concept, experimental results from the implementation of this invention are discussed, showcasing its potential for applications in quantum-enabled search engines and other undetected, single-user communication systems.

The interaction between two liquid foam layers in contact exhibits an unusual and complex friction behavior, influenced significantly by the arrangement of air bubbles within the interface. We discovered that even in the absence of liquid in the contact zone, the interface displays anisotropic friction characteristics, largely as a result of the changing geometry of air bubbles within the interface. The type of friction observed here can be likened to that experienced by a solid object and is influenced by the mechanical properties of the interacting materials. Furthermore, the arrangement of air bubbles in the contact zone leads to an asymmetrical distribution of pressures and stresses, resulting in the unique friction characteristics of the foam-layer interface.

This research proposes an advanced deep learning approach with an adaptable
loss function that incorporates uncertainty entropy to identify and exclude
anomalous samples from the training data. The method is specifically designed
for classification tasks with imbalanced data sets and is effective in skin
cancer diagnosis. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by achieving
exceptional diagnostic results on the ISBI 2017 challenge dataset, with
accommodating variations in dataset configuration.

We carried out a high-resolution ARPES study on sodium and found that the observed enhancement of its electronic mass is slightly less than expected from earlier research. These findings amplify the need for theoretical models more advanced than the random phase approximation. Contrary to the hypothesis suggesting significant acceleration of the carriers due to their interaction with spin fluctuations, our data show that spin fluctuations in sodium do not substantially impact its electron mass.

Microscopic dynamics based analysis is often necessary to verify or reject microstate-level interpretations of thermodynamic behavior, especially in cases of phase transitions. This analysis involves comparing key thermodynamic and dynamical characteristics, such as temperature, entropy, and time scales, typically calculated from simulation trajectories and predicted theoretically. One essential aspect is understanding the variation in phase space volume during a process, but this is often bypassed by referencing entropy or other thermodynamic properties. However, these alternatives can be problematic, so we've developed a method to directly address the change in phase space volume and demonstrate its application in studying free expansion. This method utilizes the Hamiltonian to quantify this change, which is shown to be feasible for thermodynamically unstable states like those exhibiting superfluid behavior or undergoing phase transitions.

This passage provides an in-depth calculation for the weights of Kontsevich graphs related to connection and curvature in a symplectic manifold with a Poisson structure. We have explicitly determined the weights of these graphs, given a tree structure, and we have further derived a recursive relationship for the weights of the associated planar graphs.

We examine solitary waves known as "nanoptera," which are observed in the nonlinear dynamics of both naturally occurring timber and artificially created diatomic granular chains, as well as weakly nonlinear systems. These solitary waves occur in the context of Brillouin waves when the amplitude of an elastic modulated wave overpasses a certain threshold, as determined by the elastic buckling instability of a layer. We find that these nanoptera maintain their individual identity, as well as the overall stability of the system, regardless of their distance or spacing. Conversely, we observe that localized modes in these systems exhibit reduced stiffness and specific frequency characteristics that are dictated by the system's non-diatomic properties, as well as the presence of nearby defects or changes in composition.

A hypothetical cosmic environment where particles interact with each other and the universe's large-scale structure is proposed to study how primordial features are affected by interactions with the universe's matter. To investigate this, the Pristine model is used as a quantum field theory and its oscillations are analyzed under the influence of an expanding universe. It is discovered that the universe's expansion generally causes the features to become less pronounced, but there's a possibility for temporary amplification of primordial features during a specific period in the cosmos. The Pristine features are found to be most influenced by the universe's matter when the wavelength of the oscillations is comparable to the universe's size of the matter's potential well. To understand the detection of such features, the interaction between the Pristine and the universe's matter is modeled using a classical cosmological collider, which reveals that the features can be temporarily amplified multiple times as the universe expands, and their magnitude can be significantly affected in this way.

Consider a graph of even order G and its complete graph counterpart K_G. A spanning subgraph H of K_G, which has the same number of edges as G, is called a "matching-free" embedding. If H contains no perfect matchings in K_G, then it is known to be part of a series of graphs, called "H-regular" graphs, which have a unique structure and can be represented by a 2-regular graph, called the "accumulator graph". A specific type of accumulator graph, called "accordion graphs", have accrued considerable interest due to their connection with quartic circulant graphs. This paper explores accordion graphs, investigating their Hamiltonicity, perfect matching structure and isomorphism to quartic circulant graphs.

We carry out a finite-time scaling analysis near the dynamical boundary in a
three-state quantum walk system. The study reveals a universal relationship between
the survival probability and time for various initial conditions. The obtained
scaling laws hold independently of any external influences and may be
experimentally verified using quantum simulation techniques.

Vision Transformer (ViT) is currently outperforming conventional convolutional networks in various image classification tasks. Nevertheless, it remains uncertain whether ViT can successfully identify visual attributes in unsupervised settings, a crucial capability for numerous applications. We have discovered that the existing unsupervised ViT models are unable to capitalize on the benefits of attribute prediction, yielding substantially lower accuracy compared to their supervised counterparts. Building on this finding, we developed the Emergent Attributes in Self-Supervised Vision Transformers (EMBERT) benchmark to measure unsupervised ViT models' capability to discover attributes in a data-driven manner. The EMBERT benchmark comprises three rigorous challenges which reveal that the unsupervised ViT models currently available underperform even the simple attribute prediction models. We propose two novel methods, the super-pixel feature extractor and the multi-hierarchical transformer, to enhance the unsupervised ViT models' capability to discover attributes, ultimately resulting in a significant 41% improvement over the baseline unsupervised ViT models. The EMBERT benchmark offers a comprehensive framework for evaluating the unsupervised ViT models' capability to discover attributes and suggests that more work is required to develop the unsupervised ViT models that can effectively capitalize on the benefits of attribute prediction.

A unified dark matter model has been developed, enabling both dark matter and dark energy to be described by a single dissipative fluid. The proposed cosmological framework, UDMS, necessitates that the EoS parameter for dark matter be less than -1, exhibiting behavior similar to a gas of "stiff" matter that experiences linear dissipation. The UDMS has been validated through two distinct routes: first, by demonstrating the model's equivalence to the $\Lambda CDM$ model when its initial conditions are specified; second, by showing that the model's solution for the Hubble parameter can be reconciled with observed data. The resulting UDM cosmological framework provides a single, fluid-based description for the entire universe, effectively addressing the mystery of dark matter and dark energy.

We offer a straightforward proof that in three or more dimensions, the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations has a critical issue in terms of stability, specifically when using Sobolev spaces and certain types of Lorentz spaces, thereby confirming an earlier study by Bourgain and Li.

Recent breakthroughs with text-to-image and image-to-image models have far-reaching implications for creative industries and activities facilitated by image-based platforms. These models can learn to capture the essence of image categories, but they also pose a significant challenge as they compete with established creators of visual content, potentially replicating their work in the process. To protect professional photographers, artists, and designers from having their styles replicated by these models, we need to determine the minimum training data required for them to produce high-quality images resembling the unique style of these creators. To this end, we develop the Stable Creator, an algorithm that constrains a latent space to adhere to a creator's consistent style during image generation, ensuring that even with reduced training data, the created images remain stylistically coherent and distinct from others. By evaluating the Stable Creator's performance, we find that it can produce high-quality images from reduced latent space data, and its use results in fewer data requirements from the creator. Furthermore, our analysis of the Stable Creator's output, aided by expert assessments, reveals that it can produce unique creations, reducing the likelihood of its work being mistaken for the original creator's body of work.

This research introduces a novel method for data protection called reversible concealment, which aims to safeguard classification capabilities while safeguarding private information within datasets. Reversible concealment allows for the stratification of data into public and private components, with the latter able to be restored once processed by a trained neural network. By achieving this, the study utilizes Bayesian Neural Networks to develop a straightforward implementation of reversible concealment, with the outcome demonstrating that BNNs can be trained in an unsupervised manner to effectively safeguard private data in datasets.

Our research focuses on the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To make J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter conceivable, we introduce a light intermediate boson with properties similar to the Z particle. A diagram representing J/ψ decaying into a Z particle which in turn breaks down into a photon and neutrinos or dark matter particles is also incorporated. In the case of neutrinos, this scenario is analyzed within the framework of an effective neutrino operator and by comparing it to search limits set by J-PET experiments on neutrinos. This shows that a neutrino mass in the range of 5-35 MeV is consistent with current experimental constraints. However, such a neutrino mass may be outside the range of effective field theory validity. To explore this, we computed the one-loop electroweak corrections to J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter. This reveals that radiative corrections could significantly impact invisible matter search outcomes. A related issue is the sensitivity of J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter to dark matter model uncertainties. To address this, we derived a precise bound on the nucleon-dark matter effective coupling from J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter within the effective dark matter operator framework. This shows that such a coupling can be constrained more tightly by J/ψ search experiments than by direct and indirect dark matter detection methods. Finally, a related experimental observation

High-resolution images from the SDO and HMI telescopes were used to study the basic characteristics of magnetic bright points (MBPs) in the quiet sun's photosphere. Employing an advanced detection method that accounts for MBPs' dynamic behavior, researchers were able to analyze their properties under different solar conditions. A statistical distribution of MBPs' brightness was observed, which could be effectively represented by two overlapping functions representing brighter and dimmer features. These findings reinforce the idea that MBPs are complex and dynamic solar phenomena that cannot be understood without considering their full dynamics.

Human vision can extract and process important information from short, acute visual recordings during events like minimal films, which are full of noise and have extremely limited durations, often measured in nanoseconds or microseconds. Effective visual systems, whether artificial or natural, must be capable of effectively handling such data. This study compares human performance in identifying minimal films with dynamic object recognition models, which are trained using deep learning techniques. These expert systems can process film data in as little as 20 computational steps, but are significantly outperformed by humans in detecting minimal films, highlighting their potential limitations in dealing with short, noisy recordings.

Dark particles interacting through Abelian gauge symmetries can strengthen existing magnetic fields within galaxies, even in the absence of standard matter magneticogenesis mechanisms. We explore the possibility of light, magnetic charges interacting with each other through the non-linear behaviour of the gauge field, resulting in an effective magnetic coupling between dark particles. The strength of this coupling can lead to an optimal mass range for the dark particle, optimal for maintaining galactic magnetic fields. For the case of interacting milli-magnetic monopoles, this optimal mass range falls within the range of peta-electronvolts, making it accessible to investigation with forthcoming particle detectors.

The rapidly evolving Earth Observatory research area has immense potential to utilize AI in real-time weather forecasting. This work addresses the challenge of accurate weather prediction by leveraging the latest transformer-based architecture, building upon existing research that utilized sequential data from weather nets and individual frame analysis. A key limitation of current approaches is their inability to harness the full information in spatiotemporal sequences, leading to partial context in frame-only and ordered inputs in weather nets, respectively. To address this, we present AWVNet, a state-of-the-art model using a novel framework that employs a fixed-sized sliding window to aggregate temporal and spatial data, allowing the transformer encoder to capture long-term context and the cross-attention mechanism to focus on relevant features. AWVNet demonstrates superior performance on numerical weather prediction tasks, outperforming baseline models by a significant margin as evidenced by an impressive 70% reduction in mean absolute error.

In models that expand on the electroweak sector, a basis can be found where the symmetry prevents coupling, leading to viable dark matter candidates. Specifically, we investigate the $S_3$-symmetric three-Higgs-doublet models that allow softly broken $S_3$ terms, determining which models can host dark matter. The variety of models arises from different arrangements of vacuum expectation values, leading to vacua with either one or two vanishing expectation values. In our research, we consider a scenario where the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry, a remnant of $S_3$, stabilizes the dark matter candidate. Our study focuses on two models: one with CP violation and another without, each consisting of a single dark matter candidate and two active scalar sectors behaving similarly to a Type-I two-Higgs-doublet model. After applying observational constraints from LUX, XENON1T, PANDA, and AMON, we identified the mass intervals in which these models can accommodate dark matter in a feasible manner. Furthermore, we assessed the potential of future experiments like CRESST, CUBES, CAMEL, and CRL to either validate the viability of these models or refute them, depending on their performance.

The PPT quadrilateral conjecture poses a theoretical framework in which a completely positive trace-preserving map from a complex matrix algebra can be broken down into a combination of unitary operations and completely positive trace-preserving maps that have minimal rank. We examined the PPT quadrilateral conjecture through the lens of operator scaling dimensions and the eigenvalue distributions of random matrices, and found that it receives partial support from these mathematical constructs. However, the relationship between these constructs and the PPT quadrilateral conjecture remains underdetermined. Consequently, the PPT quadrilateral conjecture still remains an open problem.

In cellular transport, substances like proteins and vesicles move along cytoskeletal pathways, influenced by motor proteins that advance in a non-uniform pattern over time.  This pattern is likened to traffic flow, with the difference being made up by the balance of forward and backward traffic rates. A new model utilizing an optimal control approach, with partial differential equations as constraints, has been developed to study the regulation of substance transport over complex pathways. Additionally, this framework has been expanded to account for obstacles in the pathway through a state of motion-dependent cost function. By solving this cooperative optimization problem, the transport system's costs are minimized, providing valuable insights into its behavior. A specific example illustrating the model's effectiveness involved simulating the regulation of the squid axon's transport system, including the impact of an active section with increased transport capacity.

The overwhelming quantity of data in the financial sector poses a significant
challenge, making it unmanageable for current analytical tools. To tackle this
issue, researchers employ network-based approaches to simplify the complex
datasets, which in turn enable them to discover meaningful patterns. Network
motifs, characterized by recurring, interconnected components, serve as a
relevant framework for this purpose. We introduce an accurate and efficient
algorithm for identifying network motifs, which outperforms existing solutions
considerably. To showcase its efficacy, we apply our method to financial time-
series data, casting a net, or fishing net, or NeMo (here denoted as 'Finding
NeMo'), for meaningful patterns.

In a binary system consisting of a white dwarf and a black hole, the interaction between the two occurs through the white dwarf's gravitational collapse into the black hole, resulting in a highly energetic process. To evaluate the outcomes of this interaction, we employ the relativistic equivalent of the Reuveni-Rees model, adapted for a special case involving a white dwarf and a black hole. The model calculates various features of the resulting photon spectrum based on specific mass configurations of the white dwarf and the black hole. Specifically, we consider a 1.2 solar mass white dwarf and a 10 solar mass black hole, exploring the spectral emissions in three distinct scenarios: (1) when the white dwarf's gravitational potential energy is fully converted into the black hole's mass, (2) when 10% of the white dwarf's energy is retained as gravitational waves, and (3) when the white dwarf's entire mass collapses directly onto the black hole without any mass loss. Our findings indicate that the photon spectrum in the first scenario forms a double-bumped structure, the second scenario exhibits a prominent low-energy bump, and the third scenario displays the characteristic shape of a "continuum disc wind" in the continuum spectrum. Additionally, based on the estimated luminosity, we identify the relevant time frames for observational analysis of this binary system, suggesting that such phenomena could be observable with future telescopes like the James Webb Space Telescope, potentially providing valuable insights into the local cosmic gamma-ray background.

Three-body $\tau$-decays, which involve semileptonic interactions with light hadrons and CP symmetry violations, can provide insight into these processes. Studies of these decays have been hampered by a lack of understanding regarding the hadronic part of the interaction, specifically the form factors needed to describe the hadronic component. Given the increasing data availability from these decays at present, the method for reconstructing form factors from three-body decay distributions is examined in detail. The approach incorporates terms that account for the hadronic current structure according to the weak hadronic interaction model and its variations, including the hadronic matrix element of the vector current and the axial vector one. Moreover, corrections for finite particle width and the hadronic state topological decomposition according to the isospin mass scheme have been taken into consideration in the analysis.

Jim\'enez, Becerra, and Gelbukh (2013) proposed an generalized version of the Jaccard distance called the weighted Jaccard distance. We discovered that this generalized metric is a component of a broader family, which also includes the Kullback-Leibler distance, the normalized information distance, and the Tversky measure. This family, which is parameterized, can be used to resolve issues related to zero division in the weighted Jaccard distance.

Modern motion de-blurring methods based on deep learning utilize real-world data to train their models and accurately restore blurred images.  Despite effective results, these methods are susceptible to data disparities between the training and testing datasets, which can lead to blurring artifacts in the restored image.  In an effort to overcome these limitations, a novel data augmentation technique "PBS" has been developed.  PBS generates a "blurred-for-sharp" proxy through the interaction of a convolutional neural network, enabling the expansion of training data from a single image into multiple pseudo-images.  Following training with this artificial data, the model is able to perform well even in the absence of real-world data, producing a "in-domain" model that excels at restoring blurred images with or without noise.  When combined with the "in-domain" model, PBS also eliminates the need for sharp images in the testing phase, allowing real-world blurred images to be restored directly.  Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed pseudo-blur data, with a notable 25% improvement in the "in-domain" model and 11% improvement in the "out-of-domain" model.

In the field of robotic learning, the simplest sensors, known as interval sensors or binary sensors, are common, producing a output of either 0 or 1, akin to a light sensor turning on or off in response to light. Similarly, biological cells receive external stimuli as chemical signals, translating to a cell response through various mechanisms analogous to binary sensor behavior. The dynamic behavior of biological systems, mediated by non-linear processes, can exhibit sophisticated functionalities despite being based on fundamental biological responses. The notion of a biological system learning is explored using a basic model of a biological neuron, assuming its behavior and the response to external stimuli can be predicted and controlled like those of standard robotic learning systems.

The ultrapower of any ordered set results in another set with a inherent structure, 
called the ultrapower set, which excersises a natural similarity to the original set 
originated from. This similarity stems partly from the definition itself and partly 
from an inherent mapping, called the assignment map, between the original set and its
ulpot. It has been proven that for the ultrapower of a set without comparability, 
any complete chain within the ultrapower set can project onto a complete chain in the 
original set, whereas for sets with comparability, this statement no longer holds 
truthfully. This difference in behaviour indicates that the property of comparability 
does not necessarily hold within the ultrapower set. Moreover, any complete chain in the 
ulpot set can project onto a complete chain in the original set for any ordered set, 
whereas for the ultrapower of a monotonically complete ordered set, only trivial chains 
in the ultrapower set can project onto trivial chains in the original set. Lastly, 
it has been proven that for any ordered set, the assignment map is either entirely 
injective or completely surjective, yet injective and surjective it cannot be.

Scientific breakthroughs in fields such as physics, biology, and medicine are increasingly driven by the advancement of artificial intelligence, particularly through the use of computational models. However, the process of model development is often characterized by its expensive nature, both in terms of time and resources. To effectively employ AI in science, there is a pressing need to pinpoint areas where models can be improved, facilitating targeted interventions. Profiling, the act of analyzing a model's behavior based on its training, generally serves this purpose. Nonetheless, the widespread adoption of dataset profiling is hindered by several limitations, chief among which is the absence of a unified framework for comparing datasets and evaluating their compatibility with various modeling techniques. To address this challenge, we introduce Fiddler, a novel profiler that utilizes a reference model to normalize and compare datasets in terms of their processing difficulties. Through our research, we showcase the effectiveness of Fiddler on image recognition and language translation tasks, with notable results highlighting its capacity to predict a model's performance on an unseen dataset with 90% accuracy. Moreover, Fiddler is demonstrated to identify the root causes of a model's underperformance and suggest tailored optimization strategies, which can elevate a model's performance by up to 48%.

Hadwiger's Coloring Conjecture asserts that every graph with t colors includes a complete graph with t vertices. This has been strengthened into a depletion theorem, stating that every graph with t colors contains a complete graph with k vertices, where k is close to n to the power of 1/2. This theorem guarantees that a graph with t colors contains a complete graph with k vertices, where k is close to n to the power of 1/2, except in the case where t is four and n is five. This theorem holds that a graph with t colors contains a complete graph with k vertices, where k is close to n to the power of 1/2, except in the case where t is less than or equal to four and n is less than or equal to k. This theorem confirms Hadwiger's Coloring Conjecture for graphs with t colors, where t is less than or equal to five, and also confirms a conjecture claimed by Bollobas and Simonovits that a graph with t colors contains a complete graph with k vertices, where k is less than or equal to n to the power of 2/3, in the case where t is equal to four.

This research introduces an advanced algorithm for efficiently recovering smooth graph signals through generalized correntropy, and a specific variant of the algorithm is further developed with the kernel width determined adaptively. The original algorithm was based on an optimization method that utilized the maximum generalized correntropy criterion under the constraint of smoothness, but this constraint posed computational difficulties. A modified algorithm was therefore developed by incorporating the graph Laplacian penalty into the optimization function and minimizing it jointly with the kernel width. The resulting algorithm was successful in both theoretical and practical applications, and its performance was verified through simulations.

The efficiency of metrological tasks can be enhanced by quantum entanglement, but high precision is limited by detection noise due to low entanglement fidelity. We investigate a method to improve the metrological performance of an entangled spinor interferometer by generating customized quantum states that are resistant to detection errors. Utilizing a digital holographic technique, we create entangled atomic waves with a high degree of accuracy, and demonstrate the ability to enhance their entanglement and mitigate the effects of detection noise through a quantum error correction approach based on redundant measurements.

The focus of this research is on the first eigenvalue of the first Robin problem in bounded domains undergoing a duality transformation. The study utilizes variational techniques and the direct approach to identify and analyze the first eigenfunction and eigenvalue. Notably, this analysis yields highly accurate approximations of the eigenvalue. The findings are further illustrated by considering a specific example involving the $p$-Laplace operator in a circle, where the parameter $\lambda$ and $\beta$ influence the eigenvalue in a precise manner.

Deep Neural Networks (DNN) have exhibited impressive performance in many real-world applications, but their internal workings and learning processes remain difficult to understand. In the case of Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNN), which enable models to leverage graph structure, the complex interplay between nodes and edges obscures their interpretation. In this research, we overcome this limitation by developing a novel GCNN visualization method that reveals the weighted regularity patterns learned by the network during training. By mimicking the behavior of spectrograms in signal processing, our approach provides the ability to generalize graph-based machine learning models and has practical applications in scrutinizing the efficacy of these models. Furthermore, we introduce a simple, intuitive explanation for GCNNs' adaptive graph convolutional layers, which further underscores the graph-centric nature of these models. Examples and source code are available for reproduction of the findings.

A recently developed neural dependency parsing method is investigated for its performance under low resource conditions. An enhanced self-training technique is introduced that leverages additional contextual information from a specific type of neural network model to improve the dependency parsing results in data-sparse scenarios. The enhanced technique is comprised of three key components: (1) an initial training phase using a labeled data set, (2) a data generation phase where the neural network model creates new, unlabeled sentences based on sentential structures found in the labeled data set, and (3) a labeling step where the system applies the dependency rules extracted from the labeled sentences to the newly created sentences with no labels. This enhanced technique is then repeated until convergence is achieved using a labeled sentence set. The results from our experiments with various languages, specifically Spanish, Portuguese, and Japanese, demonstrate that the modified self-training technique leads to significant improvements in accuracy and establishes a reliable baseline for our analysis and comparison of the different neural dependency parsing methods.

We've examined the transition form factors $f_+(q^2)$ and $f_-(q^2)$ [alternatively $f_0(q^2)$] for the $B\to D\ell\nu_\ell$ transition within the framework of a self-consistent light-front quark model. To to obtain the light-front wave functions, the constituent quarks are bound to hadrons using a confining gauge potential and an one-gluon exchange interaction, further adjusted by a scalar meson exchange to fit experimental values for the mass difference $\Delta m$ between the $B$ and $D$ mesons. To account for the form factors, we used the known light-front wave functions for $B$ and $D$ mesons, and computed the transition form factors while respecting $q^+\to\infty$ and $q^-\to 0$. Our results for $f_+(q^2)$ and the ratio $f_-(q^2)$ to $f_+(q^2)$ are compared with other models and experimental data. To test the predictions for several quark models, we evaluated the differential branching ratios $\frac{d{\cal B}(\bar{B}^0\to D^+\ell^- \nu_\ell)}{dq^2}$ for specific $\ell$ and derived the $q^2$ dependence for ${\cal B}(\bar{B}^0\to D

We use the example of the bosonic string to examine how branes relate to violations of time-reversal symmetry in both string theory and the path integral formulation. The string can be visualized as a two-dimensional sheet that accumulates at branes, which represent higher-dimensional analogs. The tension of branes acts as a barrier that causes the string to bounce back when it reaches them, thereby giving rise to reversible time-like reflections. However, it is theoretically possible that the branes could have a different structure that produces an asymmetrical effect on the string, resulting in an irreversible path integral scenario. Alternatively, the braiding effect of the Fock space can be utilized to introduce time-reversal symmetry violations, in which case the braides can be identified with the branes.

We demonstrate in this paper a correspondence between monadic second-order (MSO) logic and choiceless polynomial time (CPT) using symmetric, monotone, and planar acyclic multigraphs. The proof of this correspondence will serve as a starting point for establishing similar relationships between MSO logic and CPT using certain specialized graphs, such as those derived from minor-free graphs and graphs with specific forbidden substructures. Additionally, this work provides a related connection between MSO logic and the classes of decision problems defined by uniform families of monotone, symmetric, and planar Boolean circuits.

In this research, we have investigated the insulator-to-metal transition within the pyrochlore series Eu1-xBix2Ir2O7 (0.75 ≤ x ≤ 1) utilizing Hard X-ray Photoemission Spectroscopy, enabling us to noninvasively measure the electronic properties near the Fermi level. HXPS data indicate that the core levels in this series exhibit sub-2% changes, implying that Bi doping causes minimal structural distortions. However, our analysis of the Ir 4f core-level spectra reveals a time-evolving spin-flip process during the X-ray absorption and emission experiment, pointing to an underlying impact of structural distortions and Bi doping on the local spin-flip scattering mechanism. Our results are further supported by the application of the Kotliar-Schooley model, which demonstrates that the insulator-to-metal transition in this series is accompanied by an increase in the K-S parameter due to Bi doping, consistent with the observed trend.

Consider a metric space ${\mathfrak M}=({\mathcal M},\rho)$ and a set-valued mapping $F$ that maps ${\mathcal M}$ to the family ${\mathcal K}_d$ of closed and compact subsets in ${\mathcal M}$ of dimension $d$ or less. We study the existence of Lipschitz selections for such mappings, which means we seek a mapping $f$ that maps ${\mathcal M}$ to the family of $d$-dimensional simplices, and is an $L$-Lipschitz function for some positive number $L$, and for every $x\in{\mathcal M}$, the first component of $f(x)$ is in the set $F(x)$. When this type of selection exists, we say that $F$ has a Lipschitz selection. We examine conditions under that $F$ has a Lipschitz selection, which includes specific cases when $F$ is upper semi-continuous and has compact convex images, and when $F$ is a collection of closed intervals in one dimension. To study these cases, we define the concept of a regular point for set-valued mappings, which is a point where the Lipschitz constant of any Lipschitz selection is well-defined.
